en: The Master said, "I wish to remain without words. He also said, "What does Heaven say? Thus, the Great Sovereign is without words;
those who follow next establish words. Words are that by which the Way is conveyed. To seek the Way through words rather than to realize the Way through the mind is merely to cling to the secondary.
Now, the view that all phenomena are empty except for the medicine of non-conceptualization is the teaching of the Śākya clan. Huánxī [studied] this...
As for this Master, he has retired and become known as "Mo" (the Dark One). He likely intends to obscure his brilliance and efface his utility, seeking what is called "nirvana.
Whatever he says in conversation, wherever he goes, his disciples record and transcribe it;
once these have been compiled into a volume, they have requested me to write a preface. I still remember when Huankui was at Huanglong, visiting me in the mountains every day.
He generally sat in meditation and spoke little. Later, when we met again by the side of the sun (at the edge of the world), he was even more reticent and silent than before.
I knew that he was not one who took learning to consist merely of words and ears, nor one who sought to flaunt what he possessed before the world.
Thus, for Huánxī to have a *yùlù* (recorded sayings) would be superfluous; yet for me to further preface it is, moreover, superfluous. Hereafter, if one wishes to know Huán—
Regarding Huankxi: one should seek Huankxi through Huankxi itself; do not merely seek Huankxi through recorded sayings.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s Bathing Ceremony in the year of Guiwei by Zhang Jian, the Hermit of Yushan, at his dwelling in Xitang.
Catalogue of the Recorded Sayings of Master Huánxī,
Volume One:
Recorded Sayings from the Initial Residence at Ruìyán Chan Monastery in Fújiāng Prefecture.
The Record of Sayings from Huili Chan Temple on Ruihuang Mountain in Linjiang Commandery;
the Record of Sayings from Baofeng Chan Temple on Letan Mountain in Longxing Prefecture;
and the Record of Sayings from Chong'en Chan Temple on Huanglong Mountain in Longxing Prefecture.
Recorded Sayings of Jiaseng Chan Temple in Jianchang Commandery;
Recorded Sayings of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Temple on Huangbo Mountain in Ruizhou;
Recorded Sayings of Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple on Yangshan in Yuanzhou.
Recorded Sayings of Xuefeng Chongsheng Chan Temple in Fuzhou;
Recorded Sayings of Tiantong Jingde Chan Temple on Mount Taibai in Qingyuan Prefecture,
Volume II.

Small-scale sermons (xiaochan), citations of ancient precedents (niangu), verses on ancient precedents (songgu), general dharma discourses (pushe fayu), eulogies and verses for Buddhas and patriarchs (zuzong zanji song), inscriptions and postscripts (tibashi),
minor Buddhist rites (xiaofoshi), self-eulogies (zizan), biographies (xingzhuang), and postscripts.
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Huánxī*,

Volume One Recorded when Master Huánxī first established himself at Ruìyán Chán Monastery in Jiān'íng Prefecture Compiled by the student of the Way, Jué Cǐ [The Recorded Sayings of Master Huánxī], Volume One: Recorded Sayings from when Master Huánxī first took up residence at Ruìyán Chán Monastery in Jiān'íng Prefecture Compiled by Jué Cǐ, a student of the Way.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of the Chunyou era, the Master entered the monastery. Pointing to the triple gate, he said: "The entire earth is this gate; it opens wide and closes high.
Through the night there is a living path, yet with its seven holes and eight openings, when you reach this point, you must by all means avoid taking a step forward too lightly.
Why? Have you not heard it said: 'Upon entering the gate, one asks for the name'?"
In the Buddha Hall: "The Yellow-Faced Gautama has immeasurable faults and transgressions. Why, then, does Ruiyan prostrate and burn incense?
Let others say what they will of his shortcomings."
The Abbot: "From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old, they have established a nest within that which has no nest, trapping ordinary people alive with no place to draw breath.
Today, Ruiyan shall analyze this from the beginning and strip it away to the very bottom, meeting everyone face-to-face before the empty kalpa.
Is there anyone here who is quick-witted? After a long silence, he said: "Thirty years hence..."
Holding up the robe: Since the time of Caoxi, the Dharma has pervaded the entire universe, while the robe has ceased its transmission. But tell me, from where did this robe come?
From Vulture Peak in the Western Heavens, and from Huangmei in this Eastern Land.
The Dharma Seat. This seat is so high and broad that I cannot ascend it; it would stain my robes and kill me, or cause me to stumble in fear and kill me.
Today, such a fortunate opportunity is difficult to encounter. For his sake, I shall uproot [my own attachments]. Thereupon, he ascended the seat with rapid strides and, holding up incense, said:
"This single portion of incense, I burn within the burner, reverently for..."
For the present Emperor, may his sacred life be prolonged: ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! Next, holding up the incense, he says:

"This single offering of incense is respectfully presented for the Governor, Commander, Chief Administrator, and Great High Official, as well as all the honored officials of the Prefecture and the County Magistrate, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, to augment their years of official service.
Next, holding up the incense, he says: "This single offering of incense has long been cherished within my breast."
From the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, even they could not find their heads or noses; how could the old masters of various quarters know whether their breath exists or not?
Having traveled across lakes and seas for thirty years, there was only Wuzu who was slightly better than the rest. Today, I shall burn him away in this one furnace before you.
This is by no means to repay his virtue or requite his kindness, but rather to perfume the air and warm the earth. Thereupon he sat cross-legged (the question and answer are not recorded). Then...
It is said: "If Śākyamuni had not appeared in the world, all people throughout the great earth would have attained Buddhahood long ago;

if Bodhidharma had not come from the West, the ocean of lands and dust motes would never cease speaking of Chan. If you can understand it in this way, you will know that this monk has not yet left Jingwu."

I have already rubbed shoulders with the Ancient Buddha of Koubing, bare-bodied and side by side; now I have arrived at Ruiyan, where I am fundamentally one with National Teacher Guoyi, their eyebrows knotted together.
Though the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon are the same. Since the clouds and moon are the same, what need is there to speak of the streams and mountains being different?
It has reached the point where chariots and books are unified, heaven and earth are clear and peaceful, and the One Person sits high and aloof in non-action.
The myriad nations have all returned to this ultimate transformation. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "Great Peace has no form," how would you express it?
Simply observe that the imperial wind forms a single expanse; one knows not where the boundaries lie. Again, he raised the case:
A monk asked Caoshan, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? Caoshan said, "Caoshan is not as good. The monk asked, "How was it after he appeared in the world? Caoshan said:
This is not as good as Caoshan. The Master picked up [the case] and said: "Great indeed is Caoshan! His fame resounds through the universe, and his spirit pierces the ox-herd star and the Dipper.
To answer this monk’s question in such a way—this is truly not yet it. Today, if someone were to ask me, Xiu Ruiyan: "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world?
I would say: "Not as good as Ruiyan. "How was it after he appeared in the world? I would say: "Not as good as Ruiyan. One must be like this.

Only then can it be attained. That evening, he gave a small discourse: "A bright mirror stands upon its stand; beauty and ugliness appear of themselves. A hair-cutting blade is held in hand; killing and enlivening are applied according to the occasion.
If it is thus and thus, the Southern Dipper turns east and the Northern Dipper shifts west. If it is not thus and not thus, it is like the winter months."
Thunder shakes; it snows in summer. Adding to the much and subtracting from the little; giving to that which exists and taking from that which does not.
Not falling into the ordinary, it alone transcends the realm of forms. If, within suchness, one is not thus, and within non-suchness, one is indeed thus—what then?
After a long silence, he said, "No one understands this meaning; it makes me remember Nanquan. He then raised the case where Chan Master Yan of Ruiyan in Taizhou asked Jia Shan:
"In this way it is easy; not in this way it is difficult. In this way and in this way, one is alert and aware.
Not in this way and not in this way, one dwells in the realm of emptiness. 'In this way' and 'not in this way'—I ask the Master [to explain]."
[The Master] said, "The swift path. Shanshan said, "This old monk is deceiving you, Dali.
Yan shouted, "What kind of time is this for an old monk? and then went out. Later, a monk recounted this to Yantou, who said, "Alas!
This branch of our Buddha-dharma is being carried away in such a manner. The Master commented: "Ruigan was far too boastful in his display of brilliance. Yuan.
They do not understand the principles of the Buddha-dharma. For what reason did Yantou instead say, "Alas!
This single branch of the Buddha-dharma is being carried away like this"? Tell me, does he approve of them or not?

He leaves two monks to ascend the hall. This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. The Buddha Hall faces the triple gate; the lantern hangs upon the pillar.
One cannot shift or alter it by even a single hair’s breadth; one cannot increase or decrease it by even a single hair’s breadth. Perhaps someone might come forth and say:
"Elder, yesterday was the last day of the first month of winter; today is the middle month of winter."

At dawn, the nights grow longer and the days grow shorter; the sun and moon alternate with one another. How can one explain the principle that is neither shifting nor increasing or decreasing? Simply tell them:
"In Ruiyan Monastery, the administrative officers and head monks were no fewer yesterday and no more today.
Can they be increased or decreased? Each should rest content in their own station and attend to their fundamental duties; can they be shifted?"
"Mm? Have you not seen the words of the ancients: 'Without error and without forgetfulness, follow entirely the ancient statutes'?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Beside the Ice-Bath Bridge, before the Tiger-Subduing Rock; the snow melts from the tips of the pines, and spring arrives at the side of the plum blossoms.
The eyes of the ancient Buddhas protrude; the face of Gautama is manifest. Yet, if you recognize it, you remain as before separated by a great thousandfold world-system."
The Buddha ascends the hall after attaining the Way: "Night after night the morning star appears; who with eyes would not see it?
Yet this night, Old Gautama was turned by the morning star, and even unto this day his double eyes remain blurred. The flawless white jade has spontaneously developed a flaw."

The Master ascends the hall to address the two classes of assembly: "The Dharma has no fixed form; it accords with conditions as its principle. It is like water on the earth, like clouds moving through the sky—sometimes rolling up, sometimes spreading out;
sometimes to the west, sometimes to the east. Amidst the surging billows of clouds that touch the heavens, there is the news of a river clear and pure as white silk;
amidst the torrential rain that pours from overturned basins, there is not the absence of the description of a sky opening and the sun shining. Such is its function."
He possesses no such virtue; in his stillness, he does not dwell upon his own achievement. Now tell me: what thing is it that is so profoundly numinous?
After a long silence, he said: "Let the vast ocean change as it may, I shall never explain it for you."
Ascending the hall for the Lantern Festival: The weather of the Upper Yuan is warm and pleasant; everywhere, the sounds of pipes and songs shake the earth.

At Ruiyan, there is nothing to be set forth, so we simply light one or two lanterns according to our means. [The Master] makes a gesture with his whisk like drawing a bow; it resembles the crescent moon. He then dots three points, mimicking the Three Stars.
Their brilliance illuminates the myriad flowers, and their radiance swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The Vairambha wind pervades the world, yet... [text ends].
It can extinguish [all defilements]. Ten thousand *hu* of golden lotuses cannot easily be compared to it.
Blazing and burning intensely, bright and inexhaustible—yet even though it is thus, you all, in your bending, turning, bowing, rising, moving, and acting, are entirely within this treasury of light.
Why is it that ten out of ten have five pairs [of eyes] that see only pitch-black darkness before them? (He strikes with the whisk.)
The Zen chair says: "Precisely because it is so utterly clear, what is attained is made all the more slow.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the fifteenth; tomorrow will be the sixteenth. The gourd is bitter, the melon is sweet; the pine is straight, the thorn is crooked.
This old Pratyekabuddha wears paper clothing in the sweltering summer and bathes in ice during the bitter winter. He toils in vain and exerts himself in empty restraint. How can this compare to—"
Nowadays, Zen practitioners, in groups of three or two, by the water’s edge or beneath the forest trees, turn toward the fire when cold and seek the shade when hot;
who cares whether the earth overturns the heavens or the heavens overturn the earth? Even so, this jade is truly marvelous—yet one fears it may not be jade after all.
Ascending the hall: The dew is cold, the wind is clear; the mountains are empty, the moon is bright. Wild geese returning to the heavens write Sanskrit characters;
at night deep, mortars and pestles send forth the sound of autumn. Not seen by the eyes, not heard by the ears—I pour out my heart to you at this moment:
do not mistake the mountains and rivers for your own eyes.
The Ancient Buddha’s Memorial Day: Ascending the Hall. Before the Tiger-Domesticating Rock and upon the Luo River, one goes and one comes, yet there is no mark of going or coming.
Do you all wish to recognize this markless coming and going? After a long silence, he said: "Today it is the Ancient Pratyekabuddha;
in days past, it was Master Weng."
Shaking his sleeves, he ascends the hall. He holds the scales of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, commanding the humans and devas.
In seizing and releasing, in granting and withholding, each is accorded what is appropriate; in advancing and retreating, in surviving and perishing, nothing loses its rectitude.

To clarify such matters, one must be such a person; having obtained such a person, only then can such matters be clarified. Setting aside such matters for a moment—does this assembly of mine still [possess them]?
"Is there such a person as this? The phoenix and the qilin are both auspicious omens; sandalwood and the *campaka* flower are one and the same in fragrance.
Ascending the hall [he said]: A fine rain moistens the withered roots; A piercing wind stirs the forest trees. The lips of the plum have burst open to their fragrance;

The eyes of the willow sleep yet remain unsated. In the dusty world, all vie in haste and toil, As fleeting moments chase one another. For the man of no affairs amidst the woods, It is well to sing the song of the clouds.
The Gate’s Tune. As for Yunmen’s tune, how do you sing it? After a long silence, he said: "Today is the twenty-fifth of the twelfth month;
tomorrow is the twenty-sixth of the twelfth month."
Ascending the hall: Today is the auspicious festival of the First Full Moon of the Year. The rain falls in continuous succession, never ceasing.
The past Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara has, in his entirety, revealed himself all at once. Do you all see him? From the eaves, drop by drop, he is clearly and distinctly manifest.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Every person has their head atop the heavens and their feet planted on the earth; light radiates from their eyes and breath issues from their nostrils.
What need was there for the old bearded barbarian with his missing teeth to transmit the Dharma directly and exclusively? It would have been better to knock out his front teeth!
Nevertheless, were it not for the path of the woodcutter, how could one reach the home of Ge Hong?"

Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "From spring until summer, this mountain monk has passed the time in a continuous flow, yet I have not offered you even a single word or phrase for your benefit.
Reflect carefully: dwelling in the mountains in such a manner is truly of no benefit.
Yesterday, by chance, within a state of non-thought, I attained a samādhi that seemed quite extraordinary. This morning, I shall strike [the bell]..."
[The Master] beats the drum and ascends the hall. He addresses the assembly, saying: "I wish for everyone to know this. It is only you all who must attain this samādhi and maintain it well.
For hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, do not let it be forgotten. He strikes the sounding block once and says: "Do you understand? The Great Matter cannot be done for you;
each person must attend to their own small matters. Leaning on his staff, he descends from the seat.
Leaving the village, he returns to the hall. The clouds of Jianling and the waters of Jianxi are ethereal and boundless; they are deep as an abyss and bottomless.
Having gathered them all back with his whole heart, every single drop is precious. He casts them before everyone’s eyes—take care not to give rise to any deliberation. Why?
If you see it and do not take it, it will be a thousand miles away when you think of it.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Zen, Zen! Wind arises at the treetops; leaves fall before the courtyard. The chirping of cold crickets pierces the walls;
the cries of returning geese cross the Liao River sky. You people—if you can understand this, Wu Village is not far from here.
If you cannot understand it, the Lanxi waters flow beyond the Yangshu border. A-he-he! Laughing until he falls over is Zhang Daxian of Wuyi."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The bright moon of mid-autumn—its pure radiance is the same everywhere. All people are illuminated by it; there is no water that does not reflect its form.
Perfect and full, cleansed of even the finest speck of dust, the shadows of the cassia trees sway. Through antiquity and today, who has contended for its beauty?
Who has reached the Palace of the Vast Cold? Has anyone ever reached the very bottom? After a long silence, he said: "Three lifetimes, sixty kalpas."
On the ninth day, visiting old friends, he ascends the hall. It was Chongyang in years past; it is Chongyang today. The chrysanthemums by the hedge display their pale golden hues.
Do not marvel that last year my hair was like a tangled thicket, while this year half of it has turned to frost. I rejoice to have fellow travelers visit me.
The scenery over there and the scenery here—let us not weigh them against one another. Together we face the flowers to borrow a moment’s intoxication, singing aloud.
He laughs loudly; he dances with his hands and kicks with his feet. Those who follow the teachings say he is crazed and mad.
Why is it so? Have you not heard it said: "When a friend comes from afar, is that not a joy?"
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. Holding up his whisk, he calls to the assembly, saying:
"This seed of fire—before the primordial chaos was divided and before Vipaśyin Buddha was born—its brilliant radiance was already impossible to suppress.
For no reason, the old fellow Kāśyapa pointed to heaven and earth and blew upon it; Bodhidharma crossed the seas and deserts and fanned it toward the East. To sell [it]..."

Chai Hanzi was dragging a bundle of firewood when he tossed it down and fanned it up. From that moment on, there were vast movements to the east and west, and bustling activity to the south and north;

thousands of kinds of practices and ten thousand ways of functioning arose. Yet, what was intended to be made manifest became deeply obscured, and what was meant to be increased grew ever more subtle.
By the present day, it has almost come to a standstill. Dongshan shall now attempt to strike a blow within the cold ashes.
Look! [The Master] draws a line with his whisk and says: "Do you see? Although the smoke and flames are not many, one must guard against them scorching the face when they come near.

On the anniversary of the Ancient Buddha’s passing, he ascends the hall: At Tiger Creek, the ice is as clear as the moon in the vast sky; on Phoenix Ridge, the pines sing in the wind of the late night.
"How laughable and how tragic, this old fellow! His appearance remains solemn and unchanged from his former self. Do you all see him?
Having said this, he dragged his staff and descended from the seat.
He ascended the hall and said: "Kaizu stood waist-deep in snow; Changqing sat until his meditation cushions were worn through. One man [faced] an iron wall, seeking to peer through it."
Penetrating. A single person drains the vast ocean until it is dry. Penetrating the iron wall, the ocean is dried up. He emerges, performs three prostrations, and stands in his place.
"Rolling up the curtain, all under heaven is wide. How pitiable, how laughable! What is easy, what is difficult? To believe in the Way, the fragrance of plum blossoms strikes the nose;
one must surely undergo a thorough chilling to the very marrow of the bones.

On the Lantern Festival, Chan Master Xie Qi ascended the hall and said: "Amidst clusters of fine silks and within circles of lutes and songs, the Tathāgata Lamp-Light emits radiance and manifests auspicious omens.
Do you all see him? After a long silence, he said: 'He passed away long ago.'"
The Master ascends the hall to thank the attendants: "Dongshan has opened a small theater to arrange a script of episodes that neither Buddhas nor patriarchs have ever managed to perform.
Yet, a single thread does not form a line, and a solitary palm does not ring out a sound; it must be through everyone here joining together to prompt the performance that it can be realized.
This is what is meant by 'the singer sings and the clapper claps,' with strings and pipes playing in harmony, and metal and stone sounding forth."
In this exchange, the mountain monk has won; within it, he raises the grand framework and seizes the essential pivot.

Rolling up and unfolding, advancing and retreating, opening and closing, expanding and contracting—sometimes manifesting demonic faces and divine heads, sometimes extending Buddha-hands and donkey-feet—he undergoes a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, moving freely in every direction.
To an onlooker, one can only blink their eyes. Tell me, is this supernatural power? Or is it wondrous function?
It is so by the very nature of things. Do you understand? Has it not been said: "Just look at the puppets on the stage;
their every movement is pulled and directed by the person inside."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The autumn wind rolls across the earth; the autumn waters join the heavens. The shadows of a thousand mountains grow thin; ten thousand trees stand desolate.
A few notes of a fisherman’s flute rise upon the river moon; a single song of a woodcutter drifts through the mist atop the ridge.

Hearing such a report as this, you must by all means avoid interpreting it as a description of external scenery. Since you do not interpret it as a description of scenery, how, after all, will you understand it? After a long silence, he said:
The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all sentient beings.
[The Master] ascends the hall to express his gratitude to the Prior, the Librarian, the Guest Prefect, the Steward, the Head of Quarters, and the Attendants.
"Yangqi’s three-legged donkey and the sleeping tiger cub of Tiger Hill—since their coat colors are identical and their hooves and claws are alike, they gallop together across the ancestral domain."
It is ultimately difficult to construct a path toward this; one must possess the functional capacity to receive a guest when they arrive, yet strike down the feet and hands of a thief when he comes.

Only when you have the skillful application of standing with a spade planted, or carrying a spade as you walk, can you truly meet the situation exactly as it is. If this is not yet the case, [you have not attained it].
The rhinoceros horn fan raises a pure breeze; as it wafts and brushes, the fragrance of sandalwood fills the void.
[Ascending the hall,] he took up his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "At the head of the brazier, there is a dialogue concerning the absence of guest and host.
From antiquity until now, people have debated it extensively, yet they cannot resolve it. Ruiyan has a tongue like a knot and a mouth like that of a mute."
Listen now! This staff will explain it clearly for all of you. *He strikes the ground once and says:* "Three fingers up and down;
seven horses to each other."

Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "When Bodhidharma came from the West, crossing the seas and traversing the deserts to travel through Liang and Wei, what matter was he clarifying?
After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? Those who know me say my heart is full of sorrow; those who do not know me ask what it is I seek."
Record of the Sayings of [Master] Residing at Huili Chan Temple on Ruihuang Mountain in Linjiang Commandery.
Compiled by the Students. At the Three Gates, he said:
"The Gate of Unobstructed Wisdom—iron walls, iron walls! Strike once and they open, without expending further effort."
How many people can pull him back with their hands?
He occupies the abbot’s quarters: one zhang wide and one zhang high. Wind arises throughout the room; the moon rises through half the window.
When this mountain monk wishes to sit, he sits; when he wishes to rise, he rises. He never stirs up waves where there is no wind here. If you people do not...
[The assembly] dispersed. [The Master] took care to strike them with his staff across the spine. He ascended the seat;
after the prayer for the Emperor was concluded (the questions and answers are not recorded), he said: "With eyes fixed upon the clouds and the sky, there is one punch I have not yet dared to deliver.
Wandering daily through the bustling marketplace, thirty blows must wait for another time. When meeting an obstacle, I stop; when encountering a current, I flow."
Since there are no traces left in coming or going, how could there be any intentionality in movement or stillness? Yesterday it was thus:
the soaring wings flew alone, a solitary wind beyond compare. Today it is not thus: one gazes at the moon over the river, listens to the wind in the pines, and picks up Mount Geshao.
Dipping deeply into the waters of Qingjiang, I spread it out flat upon Jinfeng Island. Having captured the intent of the Patriarch, I affix it to the crossroads so that everyone may know:
in the twelve months of the year, the twelfth month is the year’s end; this is the first year of Baoyu.
Again, starting from the beginning: ten thousand years, ten thousand years, and yet another ten thousand years; the clear river remains as clear as ever, bottomless.
Even so, when the Way prevails, the Imperial Edict is not transmitted; when the times are peaceful, one need not sing the Song of Great Peace. Again, he raised the topic of Nan.
Quán addressed the assembly, saying: "The public case of Master Wáng’s lifelong tending of a water buffalo. The Master composed a verse on it:

"It is better to accept things as they are; Where among the green mountains is not one's home? Blowing the jade flute within the Imperial Transformation, Its clear melody before the wind reaches to the ends of the earth."
That evening’s informal discourse: Entering has no door; before one’s face is like an iron wall. When the path is opened, it is like pressing a gourd upon water.
Like a revolving treasure-store (dharmacakra), it is exquisite on all eight sides, turning round and round without the slightest obstruction.
It is like looking into an empty pavilion: the ten directions are unimpeded, vast and open, without the slightest blockage.
Since there is no obstruction and no impediment, there is nowhere it does not penetrate and nothing it cannot accomplish.
Whether extended or contracted, it attains the wondrous; whether unrolled or rolled up, it is free from constraint. At such a time as this, what is it like? After a long silence, he said:
"When there is wine today, get drunk today; when there is no money tomorrow, worry tomorrow."
Again, he raised the kōan of Deshan’s informal teaching where he did not answer questions. The Master commented: "Deshan took a dangerous path for the sake of a fortunate outcome;
from beginning to end, his resolve was unshakable. He was strong-willed and resolute. This monk, for his part, disregarded peril and ruin. Huiri also had a point of view:
at that time, he should have waited for Deshan to say, 'Tonight is an informal teaching where I do not answer questions; anyone who asks one will receive thirty blows.'"
He stepped forward from the assembly and laughed heartily. He taught this old fellow: he could not open his mouth, nor could he close it;
he could not sit, nor could he rise. Although it was thus, did he truly accord with Deshan’s intent?
Let any monk with discerning eyes try to distinguish this for himself.
The Head Administrative Officer (Jishi Tōshu) remained as he was; the Master ascended the hall and said:
"Since I entered this monastery, I have been busy all day long with affairs that fill every corner. Seeking the leisure of former days—how could it ever be regained?
Fortunately, my eyes and nostrils remain exactly as they were. The Main Gate faces the Buddha Hall; the kitchen faces the Sangha Hall—all remains just as it was. Monks are monks."
To act is to act. East is east; west is west. It is simply according to the old way. Even though it is so, tell me:
as for the brand-new edict, how is it? Last year’s plum blossoms, this year’s willows—their colors and fragrance remain as they were.
Ascending the Dharma Hall for the Offering and Distribution Ceremony on the Sacred Festival of the Heavenly Foundation: The great treasury of wisdom-power revolves ten billion times in a single day;

revolving ten billion times in one day, it revolves a thousand million billion times over a thousand days. By this number of revolutions, I pray to offer my congratulations upon the longevity of the Son of Heaven.
May the Son of Heaven’s life-span increase even further than the number of these revolutions. May the jade leaves flourish and the golden branches grow lush, forever united with the Dharma.
When the wheel has no end, the Buddha ascends the hall for the Nirvana discourse: Verdant willows dance by the embankment; yellow orioles sing in the trees.
The true form of Gautama is vividly present even now. Who says he entered extinction at the Twin Trees?
Offering incense on the anniversary of National Teacher Wuzu’s passing: This old fellow understands nothing at all.

Not only is he full of deviousness and crookedness, but he is also stubborn and indolent. I was ill-fated enough to encounter him in the past, and I have found him utterly intolerable until this very day.
I burn a stick of incense, prostrate three times, and exchange blows; let neither of us harbor resentment.

Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat: Today marks the opening of the retreat; the commands must first be issued. These three articles of the monastic code are universally proclaimed for the sake of humans and devas:
The body must not move recklessly, yet it must not remain as a motionless block of wood. The mouth must not speak recklessly, yet it must not remain in total silence.

The mind must not be raised recklessly, nor should it be left in a state of blank ignorance. Practice in this way and abide in this way; then the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment will constantly manifest before you.
Xie Bifeng ascends the hall and roars like a lion, speaking with fearlessness. When the hundred beasts hear this, their heads all split asunder. Thus it is said.
Then the stone dragon was struck with awe, the golden phoenix descended in a graceful manner, the waters of the Xiao River surged with waves, and the auspicious mountain rose high with its peaks;

these were not beyond what was expected. Nevertheless, tell me: when the First Seat and the Second Seat preached the Dharma yesterday, was there any distinction of superiority or inferiority between them?
After a long silence, he said: "The head of the storehouse is white, the head of the sea is black."
Ascending the hall: Awake by day, awake by night; neither restless nor dull.
What need is there to seek white jade? This very thing is gold.
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying: "The various activities and myriad expedients of all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past were intended solely for you to understand this:
winter cold, summer heat; night darkness, day light; three decades in a month, one month in three phrases.
Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he asked: "Do you understand? To call repeatedly for 'Xiaoyu' is originally a matter of no concern; it is simply..."
"The donor recognized the voice.
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall: in summer, one seeks coolness; in winter, one turns toward the fire. From antiquity until now, everyone has passed their time in just this way.
"I do not know what the Second Patriarch was ultimately seeking when he stood in the snow with it reaching his waist. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand?
Where I find 'impossible,' I learn from Liu Xiaohui’s 'possible.'"

Ascending the hall, he said: "There is no Chan to be practiced; there is no Way to be learned. It is simply a matter of each of you becoming sober from your intoxication and awakening from your dream.
Once the intoxication has sobered and the dream has awakened, although you remain the same person as before, you are nonetheless worlds apart from who you were."
Record of the Sayings of [Master] at Baofeng Chan Monastery on Lestan Mountain in Longxing Prefecture. Compiled by the Students.
Pointing to the Three Gates, he said: "All Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have entered through this very gate. Now tell me, how [do they enter]?"
This is the gate. After a long silence, he said: "If someone were to touch the pivot, both doors would swing—one east, one west.
As for the Buddha Hall: Deshan tore it down; Baofeng burned its incense. Both are not bad; both are not unsound.
Gautama was originally just a fellow with yellow skin."

Ascending the seat, he offered prayers for the Emperor (the exchange of questions and answers is not recorded). He then said: "The Dharma has no fixed form; it becomes a school whenever it encounters conditions.
The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it is only averse to discrimination. True Suchness does not maintain its own nature, but adapts to conditions, manifesting in ten thousand differences.
Far beyond the ford of the Ancient Sword, willows hang over both banks. A solitary sand gull takes charge of the peak of Du Xiu, where dripping green descends in a thousand fathoms."
Flocks of wild ducks fly; the winnowing basket of Guanghan is lifted up. Winnowing east and winnowing west, the water mill of Guansi is tested.

Pushing left and pushing right, it fosters transformation and growth within the two realms of heaven and earth, bringing prosperity throughout the four seas. All under heaven is filled with harmonious vital energy.
"The spring breeze pervades the earth. At such a time as this, where does the merit reside? After a long silence, he said: "A thousand peaks pay homage to Mount Hua;
ten thousand streams flow solemnly into the vast ocean. He then raised the case of Sansheng, who said: "Whenever I meet someone, I come forth;
when I come forth, I do not act for others. Xinghua said: "Whenever I meet someone, I do not come forth; when I come forth, I act for others. Zhenjing said: "These two..."
"This old fellow of ancient cunning has stolen a mere fragment of Linji’s livelihood; each has demarcated his own territory and boundaries, causing even clear-eyed monks to do nothing but laugh.
The Master said, "Zhenjing’s critique like this sees only the sharpness at the tip of the awl."
Not seeing the squareness of the chisel-head, even a clear-eyed monk can only laugh.
Little do they realize that these two great elders—neither brotherly nor fraternal—are contradicting themselves and utterly destroying the tradition of Linji’s school.
As for New Baofeng’s critique in this manner, tell me: does it escape the laughter of the monks? Let those with eyes discern it.
That evening’s informal discourse: The pond of Letan is limpid, soaking the moon; the treasure of Baofeng blazes forth with radiant brilliance.
If you personally reach this peak, you must surely obtain this treasure. Once you have obtained this treasure, you must immediately smash it to pieces;

only by leaving no trace behind will you succeed. If you personally reach this pond, you must immediately suck it dry; only when not a single drop remains will you succeed. Thereafter, within the state of non-...
From a single drop, clouds arise and rain falls, moistening and nourishing the great earth and its grasses and trees, yet without forming any thought of moistening or nourishing.
In a place where there is no trace or shadow, the inexhaustible treasury is opened to relieve all who are poor and destitute, yet without giving rise to any notion of providing relief.
Thus, poverty and abundance are seen simultaneously; the grasses and trees flourish and prosper, such that there is not a single thing that does not fulfill its life. There is none...
A single person might lose their place. Even so, suddenly, with this mountain monk’s whisk, I shall swallow up both Lestan and Baofeng in one gulp.
Where, then, will you all find a place to settle your bodies and establish your lives? (He strikes the meditation seat with the whisk and says:
"By no means must you depart from this very spot. Again, he cites Master Mazu, when a monk asked him:
After the assembly had entered, Mazu drew a circle and said, "If you enter, I strike; if you do not enter, I strike. As soon as the monk stepped inside, Mazu struck him.
The monk said, "Master, you may not strike me. Mazu leaned his staff against the wall and withdrew.
The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "Mazu drew this circle; no one in the entire world can leap out of it. Yet this monk responded in such a manner."
Now tell me: can you leap out?
[The Master] leaves behind the two classes of officials and thanks the newly appointed Elder Nittsū. He ascends the hall and addresses the assembly, saying:

"Of all the various arrangements one could devise, none are better than the ordinary; it neither startles the crowd, yet it endures for a long time. Since I entered this monastery, I have suffered from a cold."
Coughing is as usual; there is nothing to be contrived. One joyfully attains the countenance of the Great Master Jizu: fundamentally, it is just as it always was.
Before the eyes of the great assembly, with the head atop heaven and feet planted on earth, it is fundamentally just as it always was. Those on the east side discern the affairs of the east;
those on the west side discern the affairs of the west—fundamentally, it is just as it always was. Three meals during the day, at night...
One night, Yuan was just as usual. Although he was indeed as usual, there was nevertheless something startling within it.

Yesterday morning, when dark clouds gathered from all sides and the rain was falling in torrents, suddenly a beam of sunlight came down from the south, penetrating to the very top and bottom of every thousand crags and ten thousand gullies of Lestam Mountain, making each and every part transparently unified. One did not even realize it was the sun.
Guang is the Le Tan; Le Tan is the Sunlight. What is called "its light pervading everywhere" is neither destroyed nor mixed.
Those who see it and hear it leap for joy, all saying: "A rare occurrence! A startling feat! Although it is a startling feat, it must nonetheless endure for a long time.
How can this be seen? It is not said that the Buddha-dharma is something meager; it has existed for a long time.
"Longevity depends entirely on the person.
When the two elders Yan, Qing, You, and Sheng arrived, the Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "Open the door to await the wise; when the wise come to visit, they rejoice.
Two by two, they do not form a pair; one by one, there is no mutual interference. They lie together, yet not upon the same bed. Together...
Their actions do not coincide. It is clearly manifest before one’s eyes; yet it cannot be seen before one’s eyes. Although it cannot be seen, I alone know its reason.
Do you all know it? After a long silence, he said: "The Bodhisattva Shengrong comes from the Western Heaven;
the Immortal Lu and the man of Xia reside in the Eastern Land."

Ascending the hall for the first time after reoccupying Baofeng: Clouds emerge from mountain clefts without intention; their labor is not bestowed in vain. Water returns to its deep pool at the proper time;
the Dharma has no fixed form. In practice, one is certainly without weariness; in dwelling, one likewise feels no joy. Yesterday I followed the master as a guest.
He departs without leaving the gate; now he follows the guest and becomes the host. He arrives without entering the door.
Since he neither leaves the gate nor enters the door, his coming and going are clearly without coming or going; his distinct roles as host and guest are not truly host and guest.
Lake Ledu has always been deep and dark blue; Mount Duxiu remains, as before, towering and prominent. Even so, it is just like presenting one’s original face once again.
"Re-examining a new phrase: how about this? [He] strikes the whisk and says: 'Every beat is the command.
[He] ascends the hall to give thanks to the Administrator for the land redistribution. He cites a verse by Dongshan Yanzu: "A plot of vacant land before the mountain;
With palms joined, he earnestly asks his forefather: 'How many times have you sold it only to buy it back again? It is out of affection for the pines and bamboo that you draw [the water] in.'"
Clear breeze. Old Dongshan. Although there is freedom in buying and selling, in the end one cannot avoid joining one’s palms and asking others about it.
At Baofeng, however, it is otherwise: A single expanse of idle land before the mountain; though sought without intent, it is perfectly present.
How much of the scenic splendor has been purchased? Not a single coin was ever spent.
Ascending the hall after the retreat has concluded: Today is the conclusion of the retreat. How so? All previous restrictions are now universally lifted.
A solitary falcon soars through the autumn sky across ten thousand miles; east, west, south, and north, it flies as it pleases.
On the first day of the ninth month, he returned to Yunju. Ascending the hall, he said: "Yesterday I went from heaven above; fundamentally, I did not leave the earth below.
Today I return to the earth below; likewise, I do not leave heaven above. Above and below are without interval; coming and going are without discrepancy.
A single wild goose over the autumn Milky Way; a thousand households with their mortars and pestles at night."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the fifteenth day, it is 'the mind is itself the Buddha. After the fifteenth day, it is 'neither mind nor Buddha.
On the fifteenth day itself, it is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor any thing. To understand it in this way is to place a head upon a head;
to not understand it in this way is to cut off one's head and seek to stay alive. When it is neither of these, what then? After a long silence, he said:
Ding ren gan qian. Shang xia shi bu.

On the day the furnace was opened, the two elders from the White Pagoda and East Mountain, along with the *karmadāna* and the Daoist priest, arrived. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"When Yue divides Hu, there is something within it. What thing is this? When Hu divides Yue, there is a form within it."
What kind of elephant is this? It is as if the skill of the chisel and axe has been mastered; it resembles the rhythmic striking of the mortar and hammer.
Let us not, like Lestan, split the one into two or three, nor repeatedly mold and paint patterns. Amidst this hazy and indistinct state, let us set it aside and not discuss it.
When objects manifest as images and images manifest as objects, we shall likewise refrain from making fixed determinations. Today, as the furnace is opened, let us simply burn the fire toward it.
The Buddha ascends the hall on the day he attained enlightenment: For six years on the Snowy Peaks, I achieved nothing at all; I trained my body until its form resembled that of a crane.
Everyone says I awakened to the Way upon seeing the morning star; But when did I ever awaken to the Way by seeing the morning star? What wealth did you have when entering the mountains?
What poverty when leaving them? How many people truly know the heart?
The Head Seat Ji, the Librarian Ben, and the Attendant Zhao arrived. The Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:

"In the study of Chan and the Way, holding up this whisk constitutes the fundamental basis. If you attain this foundation, you may serve as the eyes for humans and devas and act as a model for the monastic community;
you can then unfold the entire Tripitaka or enter into the entire Tripitaka—there will be nothing you cannot accomplish. However, if..."
Not so. At the very place where a tuft of cloth is blown up, observe it with the utmost care.

When the Buddha ascended the hall after his parinirvāṇa, he took up his staff, called to the assembly, and said: "The World-Honored One, at the beginning of the Prajñāpāramitā assembly, gave this instruction:
'If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, such a person walks a deviant path; they do not see the Tathāgata.'"
One can see the Tathāgata. At the very end, on the occasion of his parinirvāṇa, he rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the assembly, saying:
"You all, observe well my body of purple-golden hue; gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied, lest you later regret it.

This old man manifested wonders to deceive the multitude; his earlier and later actions were contradictory. Since karma is self-created, there is no room for repentance once the past has passed. Thus it was said.
"Fall into hell! [The Master] struck once and said: "Today we move it again beyond the Iron Ring Mountains.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring breeze is piercingly cold; the spring rain falls incessantly. Peach blossoms chase the waves; new bamboo encloses the mist.
Xiangyan has already passed away, and Lingyun has gone too. With each deepening of spring, one feels all the more sorrowful."
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a treasure hidden within the mountain of the physical form.
That which is called hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these return to earth."
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the large and small excretions—all return to water;
warmth returns to fire; movement and turning return to wind. But tell me, where does the treasure reside? After a long silence, he said:
"The mulberry fields are glossy after the rain; The wheat ridges are fragrant with the breeze."
Incense Offering on the Anniversary of Wuzu Heshang’s Death: This old fellow—awake yet muddled; clearly without so much as a single hair’s breadth [of substance], yet insists he weighs three catties.
He knows only how to tell such empty lies and deceive others, unaware that his treachery is more grievous than the unforgivable crime of harboring a mortal enemy under one's very heaven.
As for this incense now being burned, what is its purpose? May it be that throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, [he] shall forever...
Falling into hell, there will be no time of escape.
Returning to the hall from the city, he raised the words of National Teacher Nanyue: "When departing, a stream of flowing water sees one off; returning, a valley full of white clouds welcomes one.
One’s body goes and stays, yet it is neither going nor staying; a single thing is without sentiment, yet it seems to have sentiment. The Master said, "Great!"
Master Xiaonan’s discourse splits things into two parts. Since going and staying are neither going nor staying, how could there be welcoming and seeing off?
Baofeng, however, is not like this: "Going, he goes from the red dust of the bustling market; returning, he returns to the depths of the white clouds.
For what reason is there no longer welcoming or seeing off? In coming and going, he has never moved even a single step.
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying: "The minute cannot be diminished; the great admits of no addition. It is near, at the very edge of the eye;

it is far, beyond the ends of the earth. To cling to it is error; to deliberate upon it is to miss the mark. The old bearded barbarian did not understand it; he returned to the Flowing Sands empty-handed, carrying but a single sandal."
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth Festival, he drew in the air with his whisk and said: "Written at the hour of Wu on the fifth of the fifth, All demons and evils are swept away.
Within this hall, the wind is hushed; Throughout the ages, the intent remains as it is. The *pú* grass drinks the spring snow first; The *zǒng* rice dumplings feast upon the bright moon pearl."
The tongue is like an eye; when one is intoxicated with fullness, there is no further pleasure.
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, the Assistant Abbot from Jianzhou and the Head Seat Taisou from Mianzhou arrived. He ascended the hall and said:

"The moon is in the sky, its reflection contained within all waters. But as for the moon atop the Double Sword Peak, how does it compare to the moon over the River of Hibiscus? [River of Hibiscus...]"
Last month—how is it like the moon at the bottom of Lake Letan? If you say they are the same, east and west lie on separate shores.
If you say they are different, there is no second moon in the sky. Since this is so, how is it ultimately? Have you not heard it said:
"The moon upon the cliff of white clouds, the shadow beneath the pines of Great Peace; when the autumn wind arises in the deep night, all becomes a single realm."
On the ninth day, West Hall Master Shifang arrived. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "Today is the Double Ninth Festival.
Baofeng shall ascend the heights together with you all. As the saying goes: 'If one climbs a mountain but does not reach the summit, one will not know its height.
Yet before reaching the highest point, each of you must exert yourselves; by no means may you act as if you exist or do not exist. Even if you should manage to reach it..."
From this high vantage point, one surveys all mountains as small; even raising one’s hand to touch the azure heavens is not yet possible. Why?
Because there are further sacred traces existing above.
The Elder of Yanqing arrived; he ascended the hall and said: "The rain darkens the Western Mountains; clouds fly over the Southern Ford.

Old Lu Xian wraps his waist with a saddle-cloth and rides a crane, crossing the eight-ridged yellow reeds at dawn. The flora, fauna, springs, and rocks of Duxiu Peak dance and sing for him. Why is this so?
When one's house is poor, one wishes to have a neighbor who is wealthy."
When the Buddha ascended the hall after attaining the Way, he took up his whisk and called to the assembly, saying: "Even Gautama did not understand this one point;
six years on the Snowy Peaks were spent in vain conjecture. Not realizing that it was the eye-disease seeing flowers in the sky, he mistook them for the morning star—how great a mistake!
To bring suffering upon oneself is still forgivable, but to further burden one's descendants? [He struck the meditation seat. Two rows of tears upon the coral pillow."
Half is thinking of you, half is resentful of you.
Entering the hall: The year ends and the time is spent; how many people have their feet busy and hands flustered?
Only Baofeng remains tranquil and unconcerned. Why is this? "Next year there will be new branches again; the spring wind’s vexation shall never cease."
Record of the Sayings of [Master] Residing at Chong’en Chan Monastery on Mount Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture.
Compiled by the Students. The Three Gates.
From time immemorial, the Buddhas and Patriarchs established this gateway solely so that all people throughout the great earth might grasp it.
"Hands meet in the same place. As for New Huanglong, what do you say? "I do not walk where the Tathāgata walks. At the Buddha Hall:
"I have a grievance that shall not be forgotten for a thousand ages against this old fellow with the yellow face; I truly wish to give him a sound beating with a rotten mallet.
Why, then, do I let him go today? An old man does not rely on his physical strength for capability.
The Abbot: "Occupying this room and sitting upon this seat, I shall examine each and every one—whether it be a Buddha or an Ancestor—who has come here.
Is there anyone who surpasses the Buddhas and transcends the Ancestors? Once you have been examined, you shall be struck."
Ascending with incense. Having finished offering incense and making prayers for the Emperor, he says: "In the depths of Letan, the bright moon floats;
the oars are steady and the waves are calm. Before Mount Mufu, one faces the setting sun; birds sing and flowers laugh. This is that, and that is this.
Picking it up and letting it go, letting it go and picking it up again—opening the stone gate before the Three Barriers, and wide-flinging the Three Barriers at the stone gate."
Thereafter, let those who have arrived reach the place where there is no arrival; let those who would return go to the land where there is no returning.
Those who have already passed through the barrier walk with arms akimbo; those who have not yet passed through enter by way of the gate.

To benefit what is already benefited, to act what is already done—thus they stir up the imperial wind and enjoy themselves in the sagely age. At such a time as this, how is it? Resting quietly upon the meditation cushion.
There is nothing else; the long days are desolate as we bid farewell to the Great Peace. Again, he raised the public case concerning the Three Sages’ question to Xuefeng:
“The golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net—what do you take for its food? The Master commented: “The golden-scaled fish shakes its mane and wags its tail, tossing heaven and earth;
the turtle-nosed snake spits venom and displays its majesty, surging through clouds and mist. If you all wish to know these two great elders...”
As for the place of falling: do not view the moment of ordinary encounter as something ordinary.
That evening, he gave a small discourse: "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? My ten fingers are uneven. How is my foot like a donkey’s foot?"
Four hooves tread upon the earth; every person has their own karmic affinity (*jìngyuán*). What is the karmic affinity of this Venerable One?
"Two flaps of skin for ears, a set of bones for teeth. If you understand it thus, you will see the face of the Elder Jìcuì right now.
At all times, he shares the same food and drink with everyone, sharing the same enjoyment, not turning his back on a single person, nor... [turning toward another].
A single person, moment by moment, together with all people, turns toward the second gate of meaning to discourse on the non-dual Dharma.

They do not abide in the fundamental limit, yet they do not depart from the fundamental limit. Even though it is thus, for what reason are there ten people making five pairs? They pass it by without even realizing it.
[The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "Precisely because it is so extremely clear, it causes what is attained to be delayed.
He then raised the case of Chan Master Huanglong Nan asking Chan Master Longqing Xian about "attaining the seat and donning the robe," and the Master commented:

"The Elder Jicui—what need is there for such prolixity? Initially, had he waited until [Xian] said, 'When meeting a square, I am a square; when meeting a circle, I am a circle,' [Nan] would have struck him severely."
Thirty blows! Not only will both parties avoid being caught in a mere exchange of words, but one can be certain that Longqing possesses his own distinct excellence.
On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, when the Elder of Xinghua Doushuai arrived, he ascended the hall and said: "Before leaving Doushuai, he has already descended into the royal palace;
as soon as he passes one barrier, all three barriers are penetrated. Fully guest and fully host; fully host and fully guest. At this very moment, it is like..."
"What? On the upper and lower levels of the pavilions, fire illuminates fire; as carriages and horses pass to and fro, people look at people.

The Sun of Wisdom has arrived from Xitang, and the two Daoist immortals from Penglai have come. He ascended the hall, drew a single stroke with his whisk, saying, "This stroke cuts through the clouds of delusion.
He then struck a circle, saying, "Releasing the Sun of Wisdom, it pierces through the liver and gall of the Old Lord (Laozi), making him resemble [the Buddha] Gautama."
Tán’s chest and belly are as distant as Hu and Yuè; yet they form a single unity with heaven and earth. Let this whole mass remain uncarved—yet if it is carved, it is again a whole mass.
Ascending the hall, he took up his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "It is not that you have not brought it forth; it is not that I have not handed it over.
Since what was brought forth is clear, what has been handed over is likewise not careless. But what, after all, is it?"
"What is it? He threw down his staff and said, "Each of you must recognize it for yourselves.

Ascending the hall, he said: "There is no dharma before one's eyes; it is dense and continuous, impossible to part. The meaning lies right before one's eyes, yet though one searches a thousand times and ten thousand times, it cannot be found.
When it cannot be found, it is nonetheless manifest. It is like the palmyra leaf scattered upon the head of a yakṣa; it is the peony flower."
Opening the Bodhisattva’s Face.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "When the World-Honored One first descended from birth, his three karmas were immediately impure.
With one hand pointing to heaven and one hand pointing to earth, he walked seven steps and gazed in the four directions. His bodily karma was not [pure]."
"Pure! Above the heavens and below the heavens, I alone am supreme. With such thoughts as these arising, such words being spoken, and such actions being undertaken, his verbal karma was not pure;
with his mental karma likewise impure, because these three types of karma were thus impure, he consequently experienced this extraordinary retribution.
Once every year, one undergoes the suffering of the boiling cauldron; can one ever escape it? After a long silence, he said:
"Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten. When causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself."
Xie Bingfu ascends the hall. Rain pours and rivers overflow as we discuss what is meaningless. Chen the Straw Sandals retreats three thousand paces;
Shuihuzi yields him a head’s length of ground. If anyone asks, “How is it? or “What is it like? they cannot even clasp their hands over their noses. Why?
One must absolutely avoid mistaking the old monk for something strange.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind of Nirvana and the wisdom of differentiation are difficult to clarify and not easy to realize.

It is like a thousand hands grasping different objects and a thousand eyes looking in different directions, yet fundamentally they are one body. It is like ten thousand streams vying to flow and a hundred rivers competing to pour forth, all of which return to a single water.
Although it is thus, to err by a hair's breadth is to be mistaken by a thousand miles."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the saying of Great Master Yongjia: "Directly cutting off at the source is what the Buddhas have certified; plucking leaves and seeking branches is not for me.
Having spoken thus, he has already brought up the branches and leaves. How can one directly cut off at the source?
After a long silence, he said: "The weather is hot; it is not fitting to stand for long."
Upon returning to the city, he ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday it moved, yet it never moved; today it is still, yet it never stills. Therefore it is said:
'Stillness is called nature (xing), and the mind is contained within it. 'Movement is called mind (xin), and nature is contained within it.

But what of it when both mind and nature have vanished and movement and stillness are both forgotten? A single mass of white clouds spans the mouth of the valley; several notes of distant [chanting]..."

Amidst the forest groves where birds sing, I ascend the hall to mark the conclusion of the retreat. Yesterday morning we entered the retreat; dreams were locked away and the gates of emptiness sealed. This morning we conclude the retreat; the eyes open and the heavens break into dawn.
Now tell me: is it the one who ties the knot, or is it the one who unties it? A solitary wild goose flies high, chasing the setting clouds; the vast sky is of one hue, like autumn waters.
Please, Head of the Purification Hall, ascend the hall. Let the purification bucket emit light and the tally-sticks leap about, so that all of you may reach the point of utter exhaustion.
Furthermore, what more could this old monk say? Nevertheless, there is considerable disorder here. Entering the hall:
The mind of the ancient Buddhas is just like this now. The fragrance of osmanthus fills the courtyard; leaves fall from the sparse forest. The water sinks with the shadows of cold geese;
the dew chills the night cricket’s song. An enlightened-eyed monk cannot comprehend it; those north and south of the river merely wander in search of it in vain.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: One day, because the meal was late, Deshan himself took up his alms bowl and went to the Dharma Hall.

Xuefeng said, "The bell has not yet rung; the drum has not yet sounded. Where are you going with your alms bowl? (The Master added: "He needlessly initiated hostilities. Deshan lowered his head and returned to his quarters.
(A single arrow not discharged, yet he broke the enemy's spirit from a thousand li away. Xuefeng then related this to Yantou.
(Dispatching troops for rescue: Tou said, "The great and small of Deshan have not yet realized the final word. (Using the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords.
When Deshan heard this, he ordered his attendant to summon Yantou and asked him, "Do you not approve of me, old monk?"
(One capture, one release. Yantou then secretly conveyed his intention (feigning acceptance of the surrender).
Deshan stopped; (if the lord has already surrendered, it is inauspicious to kill him). The next day, when Deshan ascended the hall, it was indeed different from usual.
(Is it so? How could it be so? In front of the Sangha Hall, Yantou clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How joyful!"
This old fellow knows the final word; no one in the world can do anything with him. Even so, he only managed three years.
(To be respectful yet lacking in propriety—how truly intolerable! The Master remarked: "Venerable assembly, this story of Deshan’s alms-bowl has been considered a marvelous mystery for generations.

In disorder, he was deceived by those two sons and could do nothing but swallow his resentment and silence.
