"Snow covers the thousand peaks—this is not yet enough," [the monk said]. "But as for the meaning of the solitary peak not being white, how is it? [The worthy replied: "It stands alone, piercingly emerging above the thousand peaks."
Externally they appear different, yet internally they remain the same;
it is never otherwise. Zhaozhou asked two newly arrived monks, "Sirs, have you ever been here before?
One replied, "I have not. Zhaozhou said, "Go and drink tea. He then asked the other, "Have you been here before? The man replied, "I have. Zhaozhou said:

"Go and drink tea. The head monk asked, "He has never been here; setting aside for a moment why you told him to go and drink tea, why did you also tell him to go and drink tea when he had already been here?
The Governor summoned the head monk, who responded with a "Yes. The Governor said:
"Go drink tea.

The sentiments of guests coming and going differ in a thousand ways; the host’s courtesy, high or low, is bestowed with one and the same measure. If you meet [the master] and do not drink, you return empty-handed;
even the bright moon and clear breeze will laugh at you.
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "The nature of wind is eternally abiding; there is nowhere it does not pervade. What is the meaning of this?
The ancient worthy then fanned himself with a whisk, and the monk attained realization.
The nature of wind is neither pervasive nor non-pervasive; with a fan in hand, one waves it at will. Before the wind, the rootless tree is blown up;
it becomes neither a mulberry branch nor a willow branch.
A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? Lin replied, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains.
Even though it is the time of the twelfth month when fire burns the mountains, this is the full presentation of the matter beneath the patched robe.
How many who have been picking through the grass and observing the wind have their eyebrows singed away without realizing it?
Miaoshan asked Yangshan, "Is it cold for you? Yangshan replied, "Everyone is right here.
Miaoshan said, "Why do you not speak directly? Yangshan said, "Just now, there was nothing crooked either."
In winter, Weijiao thunders with a clap of lightning; in summer, Yangshan lets down a heavy frost.
Two iron hammers, both without holes—having forged the universe, they naturally take their place.
Yunmen gave a teaching by saying: "Tell me, when the ancient Buddha and the pillar intersect, which level of spiritual capacity is this? He then provided his own response:
"Clouds rise from the southern mountain; rain falls on the northern mountain."
Triggering the external trigger and dispatching the middle phrase—clear-eyed monks do not know where it lands;
those who do know where it lands see clouds rising on the southern mountain and rain falling on the northern mountain.
Yunmen gave a teaching by hanging a phrase, saying: "Everyone possesses a radiant light; yet when one looks for it, it is dark and murky.
What is this radiant light of yours? He answered on their behalf: "The kitchen, the storehouse, and the main gate. He further said: "A good thing is not as good as having none at all."
The taste of salt in water is much the same; the blue pigment within the lacquer does not differ in degree.
One might say it is dark and claim there is no light, yet when looking, one cannot see—how utterly bewildering! There is no bewilderment. In the Great Peace, why must one stir up the sword and spear?
Zhaozhou asked Nanquan, "Please, Master, speak on that which transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
Nanquan descended from his seat and returned directly to his quarters. This is a public case (gong'an).

Lightning, sparks, a stone-tipped arrow, and the point of a spearhead—when the father acts in reverse and the son applies his methods perversely, their equal strength and balanced power are difficult to distinguish;
they are like a pair of unperforated iron door-bolts.
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is it like when the year has reached its end? The ancient worthy said: "The old Wang of East Village burns paper money at night;
the crow flies and the hare runs from day to night. As the winter solstice ends and spring returns, year after year—endless and inexhaustible, even the 'end' is exhausted."
At the dwelling, Old Wang of the Eastern Village burns paper money at night.

Regarding the public case of Linji planting pine trees at Huangbo’s place—taking up his hoe to strike the ground and then throwing down his excrement—how can one withstand such sky-pervading stench? Even the aged Huangbo could not restrain it.
[The Master] did so, rubbing the monk's head repeatedly.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the house style of your monastery? Zhaozhou said, "Ask in a loud voice;
my ears are deaf. The monk asked in a loud voice. Zhaozhou said, "You ask about my house style; I know your house style."
He asked about my family style; I recognized his family style. I thought he was hard of hearing, but it turns out he is deaf. Pointing south, he calls it north;
when asked about the west, he answers with the east. A-he-he! Zhaozhou is exactly like Tiantong.

I have universally taught that there is nothing external but this single, brilliant essence. The six realms of existence all arise from it. If you can know this original source, even the Buddha would not be its equal.
Do you people still know the original source? It is this very same single, brilliant essence. This single, brilliant essence—Master Mazu...

This refers to the saying, "The mind itself is the Buddha. It is what Nanquan meant when he said, "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing," and what Linji meant when he said, "There is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gates of your faces.

Though the names differ, the essence is the same; though the explanations vary, the intent does not. This is what is meant by the statement that the six realms of existence all arise from this single source.
The eye unites with form; the ear with sound; the nose with fragrance; the tongue with flavor; the body with touch; the mind with objects.
In the teaching of the Middle Way, it is said that originally there was one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious unions.

This is precisely what is meant. If you can know the original source, even a Buddha would not be its equal. Yet, alas, you do not realize this. Once you have known the original source, it remains stored within your breast.
This is indeed a great illness. If you wish to attain ease and vitality, you must forget this "knowing.
Although these six sense-gates are joined with the six objects, for those who cultivate the Way, there is no other means by which to enter than through them.
This is why Lingyun traveled extensively for over thirty years; one day, suddenly seeing peach blossoms, he immediately said: "Ever since I first saw the peach blossoms..."
Afterwards, until the present day, he has had no further doubts. Xiangyan lived for a long time at a hermitage in Nanyang;
while clearing away debris, he struck a bamboo stalk, which made a sound, and he attained realization on the spot. He then said: "One strike and all that was known is forgotten;

no further cultivation is required. Mazu once grabbed Baizhang by the nose and twisted it; Baizhang cried out in pain and, in that moment, suddenly awakened. Thus, one perceives the Buddhas of the past...
Since the time of the Patriarchs, the pathways for entering the Way have not been limited to the six sense organs alone.
As seen in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* assembly, among the fifty-five bodhisattvas, some entered through the six organs, some through the six objects, and some through the six consciousnesses;

yet when it came to their realization, there was no difference in their perfect penetration. All of you, in your daily sitting, reclining, and walking, are entirely within this very state—do not dig up the ground where you already stand.
A missed opportunity. Often people clasp their hands at their chests and instead seek to settle the matter through the mouths of old bald-pated monks on curved wooden beds;
such individuals are truly to be pitied. Nevertheless, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the Way, yet the Way is apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If one clings to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing and refuses to let them go—this is what is called "not being liberated from seeing and hearing. It is like...
The moon in the water. It was not seen. Once, while Baizhang was walking with Mazu, they saw a wild duck fly past.
Mazu asked, "What is that? Baizhang said, "A wild duck. Mazu asked, "Where has it gone? Baizhang said, "It flew away.
Mazu then twisted Baizhang’s nose. Baizhang let out a cry of pain. Mazu said, "When did it ever fly away? Baizhang [realized].

Thereupon, he attained a realization. The following day, when Mazu ascended the hall, Baizhang came forward and rolled up his sitting mat. Baizhang was like a poor man who had suddenly become wealthy; his bearing was like that of a king, yet he did not realize that the red thread beneath his heels was still unsevered. Later, when he came to attend Mazu again, while standing in attendance, Mazu looked at the whisk in the corner of the meditation seat. Baizhang said, "Using it right here; departing from using it right here. Mazu said: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with Mazu's name. The standard version of this dialogue concludes as follows: Mazu said, "What about when there is neither using nor departing? Baizhang was at a loss. Mazu struck him and said, "The one who knows does not speak; the one who speaks does not know. At these words, Baizhang attained great enlightenment. He then bowed and withdrew. Mazu called to him, and Baizhang turned his head.

Mazu said, "What is it? Baizhang said, "It is not so. Mazu said, "Who says it is not so? Baizhang said, "I am not so. Mazu said, "Who is it that is not so? Baizhang was speechless. Mazu said, "This is the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs; do not let it be lost. Baizhang then composed a verse: "The Way is originally not difficult; Just avoid picking and choosing. When body and mind are naturally at ease, Then all things are as they are. Mazu approved. He then appointed Baizhang as the head of the assembly. Later, when Mazu was ill, he summoned Baizhang and said, "After I am gone, you must go to Mount Huangbo to propagate the Dharma. Baizhang asked, "After the Master has passed away, what shall I do? Mazu said, "When you see the one with the white hair, pay homage to him. Baizhang asked further, "And after the Master with the white hair has passed away? Mazu said, "When you see the one with the white eyebrows, pay homage to him. Baizhang asked once more, "And after the Master with the white eyebrows has passed away? Mazu said, "At that time, you will understand by yourself. Baizhang bowed and withdrew. When Mazu passed away, Baizhang went directly to Mount Huangbo. There, he met the former master [Huairang], who was indeed the one with the white hair. Baizhang paid homage to him. The master said, "Where have you come from? Baizhang replied, "I have come from Mazu. The master said, "What instructions did Mazu leave for you? Baizhang recounted the circumstances of his final meeting. The master said, "Mazu’s meaning was already exhausted; why do you still ask about the one with the white eyebrows? Baizhang was speechless. The master struck him and said, "The one who knows does not speak; the one who speaks does not know. At these words, Baizhang attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse: "The Way is originally not difficult; Just avoid picking and choosing. When body and mind are naturally at ease, Then all things are as they are. The master approved. Baizhang served him for three years and then departed. He traveled to Jiangxi, where he established a monastery on Mount Baizhang. Thus, he became known as Great Master Baizhang. His teaching style was vast and profound, and he greatly propagated the Dharma. His legacy remains to this day.
Baizhang said, "In the future, when you open up these two flaps of skin, with what will you act as a person? Baizhang took the whisk and held it upright.
Nanyue said, "Is it this very function? Or is it apart from this function? Baizhang hung the whisk back in its original place.

Nanyue let out a thunderous shout; Baizhang was deaf for three days straight. Alas! Had Baizhang not possessed this final realization, he would have been unable to avoid spending his entire life [in delusion].
If one merely settles into the realm of hearing and seeing, how could there be any news from sitting alone atop Mount Daxiong?
In his ordinary room, whenever he saw his disciples arrive, he would invariably utter "Hah! or "Ho!", raise a finger, clench a fist, clap his hands, or nod his head.
Or perhaps he picks up his sitting mat and exhausts every skill at his disposal; yet even this old monk cannot help but say that such a transformation is not right.
For the most part, people depart unexpectedly—how regrettable! Brothers, when this old monk tells you it is right, it may not necessarily be right;
when I tell you it is not right, it may not necessarily be wrong. If what is held in your own hands is indeed a piece of true gold, you need not concern yourself with others.
"What does it matter whether the Way is right or wrong? Long ago, there was a monk who went to Zhangjing.
He circumambulated the meditation seat three times and struck his staff once. Zhangjing said, "Right, right. Then he went to Nanquan’s place and did exactly as before.
Nanquan said, "Wrong, wrong. This is driven by the power of the wind; in the end, it will fall into ruin. The monk said, "Zhangjing says it is right, and..."
Yet why did he say it was not? Nanquan said, "Zhangjing is exactly right; it is you who are wrong.
This is because this monk’s illness lay in the realm of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Nanquan lightly pierced through it for him, leaving him with no further recourse.
It was not that Nanquan forcibly changed him; rather, it was simply that the monk had not yet reached the state of liberation from seeing and hearing. Therefore—
The Way. One who stands atop a hundred-foot pole has indeed gained entry, yet it is not yet the ultimate reality. One must advance further from the top of that hundred-foot pole;
only then will one’s entire body be revealed throughout the ten directions of the world. Is there anyone here who can advance from the top of a hundred-foot pole?
If there is, come on a day when the plaque is displayed and reveal yourself.
In this Dharma discourse, I show the purity of Elder Mingyue.
Prior to Baizhang, there were no affairs of formal monastic administration; they tilled with knives and cultivated with fire, passing their time in seclusion. When students heard of this—

They took him as their teacher. Master and disciples relied upon one another, diligently investigating their own fundamental matter. Enduring toil and suffering, they did not alter their original resolve.

Once their power of aspiration was firm, the Great Dharma was clearly realized. They guarded it deeply and secretly, unwilling to offer it lightly. One day, compelled by others, he sat upon the *kurruka* chair;
naturally, a brilliant radiance flourished, illuminating a thousand ages. This is what is called the "Root."
When the foundation is firm, the branches and leaves flourish. Since antiquity has long passed, the human root has become increasingly superficial.

As soon as one enters the ranks of the monastic community, one immediately conceives the thought of establishing a permanent residence. Once led astray by others, one beats the drum of self-importance, acting according to one's own whims and caprices, and repudiating the law of cause and effect.
When their conditions eventually exhaust themselves, their conduct becomes deficient in ways that are beyond description. This is largely due to the failure of their original resolve.
It is not rooted in the Way; one is merely led astray by fame and profit. To err by a hair’s breadth is to be mistaken by a thousand miles.
Elder, you left home at an early age and traveled on pilgrimage at an early age; you have already traversed every monastery and retreat.

Now that the time has come, it is certainly not beyond your capacity to take up the axe for dwelling in the mountains. However, whether a monastery is large or small, its flourishing depends on the person. If, following the tradition of the ancestors—
Taking the Buddhas and Patriarchs as your standard, practice with earnest diligence; even when eating before the holy monks, you will have no cause for shame.

Why worry that donors will not praise you, that your reputation will not be fragrant, that the dragons and devas will not grant their protection, or that the four debts of gratitude will not be fully repaid?
If one acts in this manner, they are called an "Elder"—is this not for no small reason? The three scriptures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs have been sent; [read them] every day.
Having found leisure, I have read through this once; may you practice it accordingly and transmit it to others, so that you do not disgrace your status as a descendant of the Yellow-Faced Old Man.
My most sincere wishes! My most sincere wishes!

Shishi’s attendant said, "The Way lies within the midst of daily activities and constant practice. However, it is certainly not possible to take daily activities and constant practice themselves as the Way;

yet, it is also impossible to seek the Way apart from daily activities and constant practice. Whether seeing, hearing, speaking, or moving, whether eating, drinking, rising, or reclining—there is [no other way]."
One may be deluded, yet there is not a single instance that is not so. It is not swayed by the breath of vital energy, nor is it plundered by external objects.

One does not take extensive learning and wide vision as one’s own understanding, nor does one mistake wondrous words and subtle phrases for the fundamental inquiry. Appearing as if stunned or like one who is simple-minded, one simply maintains a state of tranquil stillness.
Like a wild goose crossing the vast sky, its shadow sinks into the cold water; the goose has no intention to leave a trace, and the water [remains clear].
There is no heart that harbors lingering shadows. Consider the former Zhaozhou Wenxuan: when he contended with the inferior rather than the superior, it was like gold being traded for gold.
National Teacher Danyuan’s three calls and three responses were like water meeting water.

Even if you attain such a state, you must further know that within the gate of the patch-robed monks there is a single stroke that neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can manage; only then can one enter the demonic and enter the Buddha, without [hindrance].
Whether permissible or not, whether acting contrary to or in accordance with the flow—these are all skillful means. Nevertheless, one must truly break into a sweat once before it can be attained.
If you can indeed break into a sweat once, then what Baiyun said—that upon a single blade of grass one manifests jade palaces and crystal towers—is no empty talk.
Guoguo, you have served me for two lifetimes, exactly half a decade; burn incense and ask.

Upon examination, there is no error whatsoever. Furthermore, one can spur oneself further upward; not only will this allow one to join shoulders with Wenyuan and Danyuan, but it will transcend them by a whole head of ground.
This is precisely what is required for the moment of parting and serves as a warning for daily life. It was because he requested it that I spoke these words to him.
The Ancestral Master’s coming from the West was shown by Longwei Na as a separate transmission outside the teachings; not establishing written words, he held up the single point alone,

desiring nothing more than for people to cast away the objects within their chests and exhaust the mental machinations of their daily lives, so that they might realize their own segment of radiant light, which extends—
Extending from antiquity to the present, it illuminates heaven and earth. It does not increase when dwelling among the sages, nor does it decrease when abiding among the common folk.
It is not obscured by night, nor is it made bright by day. Ten suns cannot gaze upon it; a thousand hands cannot cover it. This is what is meant by "Chan that is not Chan."
This is precisely what is meant by "the Way and non-Way. To seek elsewhere apart from this is much like going to a river to look for water, or abandoning a lamp to search for fire.
This is why the old man Kāśyapa, after six years on the Snowy Peaks, as soon as he beheld the morning star, immediately said:
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize them.
Look closely: even now, wearing heavy robes while traveling and carrying a bundle on your journey—this too is a deluded thought.

To travel up and down the Yangtze River, seeking teachers and inquiring after the Way, is a deluded thought. To sit facing the wall all day long until the grass mat is worn through is a deluded thought.
To attend morning services and seek instruction at evening, neglecting sleep and forgetting to eat, is a deluded thought. If you do none of these things, you must be a person of fierce resolve;
as soon as you hear it mentioned, you must be like a hawk seizing a rabbit or a falcon grasping a pigeon, opening your chest to receive it with total commitment.
To carry this burden with bare hands is not considered beyond one’s capacity; yet, even though it is thus, you must by all means avoid sitting here.

You must further know that there is a moment for turning about before you can succeed. Therefore it is said: "The person standing atop a hundred-foot pole, though having gained entry, has not yet reached the truth.
One must advance further from the top of the hundred-foot pole; only then will the entire body be revealed throughout the ten directions of the world."
Now tell me: at the top of a hundred-foot pole, how does one advance? Have you not seen it?
One day, Master Xinghua said to the *weina* Kebin, "Before long, you will become a teacher who proclaims the Way. Kebin replied, "I will not enter this protective community.
Xinghua said, "Do you enter it after having understood, or do you enter it without having understood? Kebin said, "It is not like either of those. Xinghua...
Hua beat him and said, "Venerable Kebin, you were defeated in the battle of Dharma; pay a fine of five strings of cash and provide a meal of steamed rice for the assembly.
On the following day, Xinghua struck the gavel and declared, "Venerable Kebin, you shall not eat this meal; you are hereby dismissed from the monastery.
Now, in Xinghua acting in such a manner, what was his intention? To benefit others, one must do so thoroughly; to kill, one must kill completely.
Seeing blood—when Kebin acts thus, what then? When the road is long, one knows the strength of the horse; when years have passed, one sees the true heart of man.
Nevertheless, even at the top of a hundred-foot pole, both have yet to take the next step forward.
I tell you, Attendant Zong, that in our school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. When the old fellow Deshan speaks thus, he has already left quite a mess.
Since there are no words or phrases and not even a single dharma, after all, what constitutes our school? If...

It is not a place where a paper candle can be extinguished by a breath; it utterly destroys the livelihood of the house of ghosts. How could one possibly establish a new way of life with empty hands and bare fists?
With a single white staff, they strike even if it be a Buddha, and they strike even if it be an Ancestor. This extends to tearing down the Buddha hall and dispatching the Arhats.
Their realization is precise and their application is expansive, like a swift thunderclap or a rapid wind that shatters mountains and shakes the seas. It is without compare.
There is no place for you to draw near, nor any place for you to look askance. How could those of shallow roots in these recent times, such as Śaṅkara, ever hope to approximate this?
Fu said: "Those who wish to emulate Yan Hui are they not his disciples? If one belongs to the ranks of the eminent, they stand like a wall ten thousand fathoms high;
they travel a thousand *li* in a single day, disregarding gain or loss and remaining unaware of peril or ruin. They set their course with broad limits, yet act with urgency.
Apply yourself with diligence, vowing to achieve thorough realization and reach the ground where Buddhas and Patriarchs have not reached, to see that which Buddhas and Patriarchs have not seen.
Stand out alone and act independently, your solitary style majestic and formidable, like a lion emerging from its den, crouching on the ground and roaring so that the foxes all vanish from sight.
Even if Zhou Jin’gang were to return to this world, he would surely yield the preeminence to you. You must strive toward this with all your heart.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs praised the manifestation of leaving the mountains, saying:
"When Heaven intends to entrust a great mandate to one's person, it must first distress their mind and will, weary their sinews and bones, and starve them."

This is not so. How could it be that for more than two thousand years, throughout ten billion sets of four continents, people have looked up to him as they do to the sun and stars, and loved him more than their own parents?
Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of hearing illuminates perfectly throughout the space between the sun and moon. His compassionate vows are vast and profound, clothing all within the four seas.
His skillful means and wisdom are perfectly integrated; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are free from any obstruction. He alone wanders with ease among humans and devas. This is...
Thus he is named Avalokiteśvara. The maiden of Malaya opens the clouds over India;

the moon shines upon the golden sands. Heart-mind after heart-mind is the wondrous Dharma; thought after thought is the lotus flower. It is not necessarily by means of the physical body [that one attains this].
Permitting the Ma family:
In the fish basket, the *bala-lan* holds living, glistening scales; held aloft in the wind, it is raised without reluctance. How many times has it circled the entirety of Changsha?

In the marketplace, when there is no one to buy from those who sell, Mañjuśrī may take grass for clothing or a lion for a carriage; he undergoes a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, yet there is no second Mañjuśrī. Nevertheless, if one seeks him...
It cannot be grasped. The colors of Mount Wutai are like suchness itself.

When the Cloth Bag meets someone and begs for a single coin, the contents within the bag rival the wealth of a rival kingdom. It is not that his descent into this world was late; it is that he detests the Buddha and refuses to act as one.
Bodhidharma came ten thousand miles from the West, crossing the northern waters on a single reed. He claimed he had come to transmit the Dharma; yet, did he ever actually transmit anything?
Vimalakīrti.

Possessing the stern air of Bo Yi and Shu Qi, and the carefree demeanor of Yan Huang and Zhong You, he recklessly creates calamity for the land of India and rises as a pest to the gates of the Śākya school.
With his mouth flapping and chattering, he exhausts thousands upon ten thousands of words, yet in the end, he does not know there is this one solution.
Everyone says that the Tathāgata Suvarṇaśālī has manifested in Vaiśālī; I, however, say it is simply an elderly Brahmin who, having suffered much illness, is well-versed in the natures of medicines.
Chan Master Huangbo Duanji possessed a vast and majestic great capacity;
his great function was unrestrained in all directions. When he needed to grasp something, he would grasp it at once, and the Son of Heaven emerged directly from within his palm.
When it was necessary to strike, he struck; the Great Tree of Northern Ji. From the tip of his staff, he sprang forth to life. Within the Great Tang Empire, there was but this one man.
For a thousand ages he is looked up to, as bright as the sun and moon.

Prime Minister Pei exclaimed, "This wretched scholar! He is truly intolerable. Wielding my spear and entering my borders, he has extinguished the Great Treasury of Perfect Enlightenment and dried up the boundless ocean of meaning at Mount Gui Peak.
Wherever he goes, all are defeated and retreat upon hearing his reputation. At the end—
Later, he encountered Boshan, who captured him with his incriminating goods and defeated him. He surrendered and submitted, vowing to become a disciple and serving him without slackening.
Master Xuefeng Zhenjue played out the "tortoise-nose snake" and struck up the "Guangling Melody. Its pure resonance is impossible to conceal; its poisonous breath is impossible to touch.
Beholding it is never enough; listening to it is never enough. For ten thousand ages, this is the blessing of the City of Fortune.
The morning sun pierces through a single tattered robe—crooked and devoid of thread. With a mere half-inch of knotted needle, he mends the nose-piercing hole until it is restored to perfection.
A single fragment: Lifting one’s head, the red sun reaches the heart of heaven.
Facing the moon, I finish the remaining sutras;
the ancient teachings only serve to shield these aging eyes. The silver hare does not realize it has ascended the solitary peak. Looking, looking until there is nothing more to see.
The Place: Light and Object Both Forgotten. Volume One concludes here.
Verses on Buddhist Activities within the Marketplace.
How many times have I wandered through alleys and traversed the streets? Selling the "Tianzhen Pearl" from the South. I have emptied out my entire basket;
does anyone know how to offer a price for it?
For over thirty years I have lived beyond the mundane world, roaming upon the seas; I have never easily cast my golden hook.
Yet, when I casually cast my line, shrimp, crabs, fish, and dragons are all gathered in a single net.
Pine winds carry the melody as the Great Officer’s sighs shake the azure heavens; its lingering resonance, desolate and wild, enters the courtyard.
It conveys the spirit of the "High Mountains and Flowing Waters," yet one knows not who can truly hear it within their own eyes.
Lotus dewdrops leap like pearls;
the *utpala* flower first reveals its round leaves. Scattered bright beads race across the azure platter. Do not compare the *hang-hsai* nectar to common fish eyes;
It is easy to behold when seen, yet difficult to find when sought.
Within the myriad differences of daily life, Elder Ding remains as immovable as space. Though spring’s splendor and autumn’s stillness undergo countless changes,
this old man has never altered his ancient countenance.
In the ancient hall,
prior to the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, rafters and beams were set upon the void; until the second year of the Jingding era,
the dignity of its former style remains solemnly intact.
The round mirror is not like the lotus leaf; the vast, open void is difficult to compare with. Within this, all is transparently empty—there is not a single thing.
Where could one even attempt to sweep away dust?
A wild boat drifts afar, light as a single reed; above and below, the water and sky are like a mirror free of dust.
Since the return of the blue-eyed barbarian, who could have known what kind of person it was that set foot here?
The moon over the bay shines solitary and clear, its curves winding and distinct; its hue is indistinguishable from the reeds. For the most part, boats return empty-handed;
how few have personally witnessed the return of the pearl?
Perilous peaks lean and tilt amidst the misty haze; their jagged edges and sword-like blades allow for little room to contend.
This central point is no mere summit for passing through to the profound mystery—take care not to proceed upward with a coarse mind.
The lazy ox has snapped free from the nose-rope and wanders unrestrained. With more than enough indolence and more than enough stubbornness, he pays no heed at all to the fragrant grass before him;
sleeping amidst the clouds and reclining upon the moon, he remains simply as he is.
Beyond the misty waters lie one hundred and ten cities to the south of the window; the eight facets of its crystalline clarity open spontaneously from heaven.
With ease, it cuts off east, west, north, and south, as infinite fragrant breezes sweep in upon it.
The empty boat is empty within and empty without; it employs no oars or paddles and unfurls no sail.
Let it drift eastward or westward as it may—who cares about the black winds that rage across the heavens?
Mount Tanseng was not yet high, nor were the waters deep; what is base is not mud, and what is noble is not gold. From the outset, I have viewed all with a single kind of equanimity;
until my old age, how could I ever have had two minds?
Kaoshan bowed three times, rose, and stood in his place. Lofty and solitary, he did not stand level with the other peaks.
Since returning after attaining the marrow, he has seen heaven and earth, the universe itself, appear low.

Entrusted to Xuedou Hisou, the tip of his tongue surges like a thousand-fathom cascade of snow; his eyes are as clear as a brocade mirror, a single vessel of ice. Such is the breeding ground for blind donkeys!
Extinguish the authentic lamp of Lingxiao’s succession!
A single vine of snow-stillness from Tianning,
reaching toward the heavens like a gourd in autumn. Blooming slowly within the ninth month, it bears fruit before the frost as vast as Mount Sumeru,
overwhelming the five houses of the East and West Zhejiang.
Behold Shituan’s words:
their language is hard and pure, like raw iron; his eyes are brilliant and lofty, dazzling like the sun. Today, there is no such work among the rivers and lakes;
it makes one sigh three times, longing for Pingqiang.
Seeing off a monk traveling to Mount Nanyue:
"In one gulp he swallowed the Buddhas of the three periods; lately, there have been many Buddhas appearing in the world. On my behalf, inquire after Old Sida.
Why is it that he cannot open his mouth for this matter?"
Regarding the price of rice in Ilüling, Zhejiang, by Master Yuansheng of Jizhou: there is no contradiction; half say it is low, half say it is high.
To make this matter complete, seal your mouth; listen as Jiangzhe clamors on and on.

Master Qiong goes to Hangzhou, carrying within his breast a singular marvel of jade and crystal. His entire being is rich and noble, yet few know it. Having smashed the four rattan canes to pieces, he gathers them up again;
spreading them out in the imperial capital, to whom will he sell them?
The Venerable Ryō of Fūhan traveled through Zhejiang, always maintaining that "the wind and banner move in the mind. Under Jiyun’s staff, this was already made clear.
Now that he has departed for the lands of the Hundred Yue and Three Wu, will he consent to listen to the clatter of another’s hot bowl?
Moonlight on Mount Song, Master Shangren, in Hangzhou;
the moonlight is like water, the night is deep and still. A single melody from the flute, its tones more refined and clear. When the music ends, do not say it has vanished;
in the after-night of West Lake, it will be even more worth listening to.

The tradition that the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the West has deceived people into digging through the earth to seek the blue sky. Moreover, now the maple leaves fall and the Wu River is cold;
go on, go on—do not easily moor your boat.
For a moment, one arrives riding the whale to seize the moon; do not decline the toil. Journey once around the ends of the earth and the horizons.
When the night comes again and one has dredged it thrice, the blue sky is clear and the single orb stands high.
Seeing Off Attendant Tan Returning to Ganshan:
I am too lazy to see him off or welcome him back before others. He departs lightly upon his path, his person unburdened. If anyone asks for a verse upon his arrival home:
"The rain has passed over Xiangxiang; the autumn moon is bright."

Diao Nie, Huang, and Chen—the two masters—held their razors and tweezers as they visited the śramaṇa. With hands joined in reverence and palms uplifted, they spoke with warm smiles, discussing the subtle and wondrous points of their craft:
"In this work, not even a hair’s breadth may be allowed to remain."
The two hands are as harmonious as the two eyes; casually, they sweep away the dust from the crown of the head.
How many men with iron foreheads and copper heads have all been pressed down by this fellow!

Ritual at Sushan Pagoda (II) The events of the year the pagoda was built have been passed down by word of mouth until this very day. To reveal the intent of a thousand ages to people, he gave two or three pieces of gold to the craftsmen.

The speech of Mount Luo cannot be grasped; who knows the heart of the short uncle? With a single incense offering he comes to pay his respects; will he deign to look upon the depths of the white clouds?

The river stretches like a single level scroll; the mountain colors are green through all four seasons. The water is sufficient and firewood still abundant; though many people are there, the cooking fires never cease.
Though stringless, the lute still resonates; how many with ears have ever heard it? The cypress trees by the eaves of Qi are withered; looking at them often, my tears suddenly fall.
Fuzang, Abbot returning to Jiangxi: My breast holds ten thousand scrolls;
both tongue and brush possess the eye of discernment. To critique the present and discuss the past—how many do you know?

What? For a hundred years in silence, his bones have not yet grown cold. His descendant stands out with exceptional vigor and surges upward. Possessing profound depth and refinement, he appears as if unable to speak;
he conceals his brilliance and polishes away his luster, dealing only in the dry and the hard. He does not learn from his grandfather by entangling himself in complications.

Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, when he utters a single word, even Buddhas and patriarchs would have no place to open their mouths. At times, his silence is profound and deep; it encompasses the entire world.
Difficult to point out or define: with the tip of his toe he topples Mount Lingxiao; brandishing his sword, he brings the dragon from the bottom of the river to life.
Beneath the three wooden rafters lie the four worlds; by the side of the broken meditation cushion is the Tuṣita Palace. When the autumn wind suddenly rises, the longing for the old mountain stirs;

returning to the source is itself no place of return—what words remain? Those on the rivers and lakes, rubbing their foreheads in anticipation, surely gaze toward you. Do not become a weight that falls into a deep well.
As I was about to depart for Xuefeng, I showed this to Master Gui.
The Master said to me, "Go away and travel on pilgrimage; I too shall go traveling on pilgrimage before long. Whether at the ends of the earth or the corners of the sea, we may meet again;
with rice from our bowls and a few stalks of radish, we shall gather once more. I laugh at myself, having reached the age of sixty-seven, my eyes dimming, my ears deafening, and my feet...
Powerless; unable to cope with anything, one merely faces a blank wall. What benefit is there in a hundred thousand regrets? One should spur oneself on while young and strong to study the Way.
Disregarding danger and ruin, advance boldly straight ahead. Like a single man facing ten thousand enemies, break the firm and blunt the sharp, achieving total success.
Letting loose the oxen and returning the horses, all affairs come to rest. How wonderful are these days of peace and no trouble! [In] the north of the passes...
Returning geese cut through the mist as they fly; the wild waters of Jiangnan stretch to the heavens, a deep azure.
Upon seeing the attendant, he requested words for a path into the Way.
There is no path into the Way. Why do you not reflect upon that which manifests in your daily activities? Having already deviated by bowing and inquiring after my health.

Tense! When responding to guests and friends, he never concealed anything; sharing from the same bowl and eating together for three years—how could one know that so many thousands of words would break out in conversation?
Today, as I burn incense to seek his words again, all those long years of gathering have become in vain. This old monk can no longer bear the distress;
I shall not shrink from striking him with a painful palm right in his face. Let him go out the door crying out in pain, calling to heaven in lamentation.
*Ma*: Teeth lost, tongue bald, mouth not yet closed.
A postscript on the verses for the Layman Guan Yingshu by Miaoxi.
Guan Gongying’s elder brother resides at Luhu. Fortunately, he has not yet been entangled and toppled by the creeping vines;

yet, without cause, he has mistakenly entered a grove of *huapu* trees, causing his entire body to be covered in thorns. The clever hands of the world have been unable to provide a skillful resolution, instead adding to it with rotten kudzu, so that the spreading creepers become increasingly severe.
Fearing that Xiu might likewise fall into this trap and find no way to emerge with sharp distinction, I have therefore—
Brandishing the precious sword of the Vajra King, he said:
"A verse by Baguyan (Baku-gan) sending Miàofēng (Hui-miàofēng) back to Nanyue:
In the past, the Elder Miàofēng carried the authentic seal of Nantáng; he surveyed all quarters with the gaze of a tiger, yet the monastery where he dwelt was but withered grass."
His ruined dwelling could barely shield him from wind and rain; others could not endure such hardship, yet the Master alone remained at peace within it for thirty years, never altering his joy.
I once ascended his hall and always regretted that my human realm was so unequal to his.
Now, observing the words he spoke to Gu Yan as he returned to Mount Heng, I see that this is no less than a prophetic transmission upon a sacred mountain. Alas!

As the *karmadāna* (vinaya-master) of Long, you have polished the hair-relics of Master Gao Yuan so that they turn like jade and revolve like pearls, scattered across a golden platter. These are the *śarīra* shown by Master Gao Yuan to others;
since you, the *karmadāna* of Long, are able to treasure them, I hope you will not allow them to be mixed with common peas or the eyes of fish. This would be excellent.
Bachi Jue’s Dharma Words for His Successor, Elder Ming (who formerly served as the *weina*):
"An adopted son does not need to be taught how to fall into error; he naturally understands the words that would fill pages and scrolls.
How could it be otherwise? At that time, the master’s staff with which Xinghua struck Kebin was fortunately not in the hands of anyone else."
Why have I been so remiss? Had I been able to put this into full practice, Mount Yu would not have reached its present state today.
Now, because the Zen practitioner Yü has brought this request for my words, I have burned incense and examined it; I truly regret it for the sake of my elder brother.

Eulogy for the Axis of the Buddha’s Tooth Relic Enshrined by Layman Zheng of Zhongzhou The Buddha’s tooth relic is a rarity in this world; it was kept with extreme secrecy in Zhongzhou. Only Master Xuanwu revealed its presence to others.
Whether the assembly at Xuefeng praised him or reviled him, it was nothing other than painting the void with five colors.
As for that which cannot be reached by praise or revilement, I ask you, Layman, to speak of it.

I have seen the writings of the attendants Wuzhun and Chijue regarding their former travels to the gates of Zhongfu and Lingxiao; seeing their proclamations, they reviled the Buddhas and patriarchs as if they were nothing more than dust, chaff, and husks.
Now, observing this letter to Nanping, I revere and love it; it is truly beyond compare, even surpassing the auspicious qilin and the rare phoenix.

I simply do not know whether veneration and affection or scolding and rebuke are the correct approach. Since you have come to treasure this [text], you should uphold it and seek out those with the "eye" at the crown of their heads to verify it;
in this way, you may see how the two great elders applied themselves, far transcending ordinary sentiments.
Otherwise, what benefit is there in a gathering of rats over dried ginger?
Following the Dharma Words of Ba Fojian Fohai:

My father and elder brother were often ill in their past lives; they were quite familiar with medicinal properties. Although the prescriptions they spoke of differed from one another, upon careful examination, all were proven effective through experience.
If one compiles and prepares them according to these, there will certainly be no error. If one does not follow this...
Even in its compilation and transcription, there is no error. Why? Because as soon as it takes form upon paper and brush, it is already no longer the sublime secret.
When Master Han said that his books should be burned, I say the same of this scroll.
Postscript to the Calligraphic Remains of Master Zhu Wen-gong of the Xunzhai:
In the summer of the Ding-si year, when the heat was at its peak, I sat in quietude after my midday meal within the "World of Grains.
A great bhikṣu named Zhou approached me with palms joined and said: "My ancestor Yungu and Master Zhu Wen-gong of Huia-ch'an were—"
Regarding his outward relations with others, Master Wen inscribed the name "Not Without" (Buwu) upon his study. Many years have passed, yet its meaning has not been heard.
I pray that you will explain it for me. I said: "Sit, and I shall speak to you. I am no scholar of the Way; how then could I explain the meaning of 'Not Without'?
Nevertheless, since you have raised this intention and come to knock at my door, enter my room, and extend this inquiry, I shall respond."

Can it not be said that these are not non-existent? My son, throughout the twelve periods of the day—whether walking or turning, bowing or looking up, laughing or scolding, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, responding or retreating—can it not be said that these are not non-existent?

On the third, eighth, fifteenth, and other such days, when ascending the hall or entering the inner chamber, bowing deeply with palms joined, tucking up one’s robes to enter the corner of the room, seeing with the eyes and hearing with the ears, the mind opens and the intellect is liberated; can it not be said that these are not non-existent?
It is not that there is nothing to it. Duke Wen had not yet recorded it; your ancestor had not yet revealed it. Yet the name of "not non-existence" cannot be hidden away.
You have not yet raised the question, and I have not yet answered it, but the meaning of "not non-existence" already stands clearly before us.

It was only upon the appearance of writing that [the truth] was revealed; once revealed, it was requested; and once requested, it was explained. It is not that there is nothing, yet in its non-being it is not nothing.
Amidst this confusion of right and wrong, it is almost impossible to distinguish them. As for seeking what is called "not nothing," I do not yet dare to guarantee it.
I await the appearance of Ajita in the world and shall request to go to him and ask. The boat suddenly rose up once more.
He bowed and said, "I have understood the meaning of 'not being without. I beg you to write this down as a testament. Thereupon, he wrote it.
This was inscribed after the calligraphic works of the various elders, including Fozhao.

On a clear autumn day following a rain, the wind is pure and the myriad valleys resound with the sound of waterfalls; the fragrance of agarwood wafts through the air. At such a time, one stands with sword held horizontally.
He was asleep when a guest knocked at the door. He called for a servant to see who it was; it was the Chan Master Yuan of Nanpu.

Yuan bowed his head in greeting and presented a large scroll. As they unrolled and examined it together, he felt as though he were suddenly meeting Zuo’an, father and son, and the great masters Juefan and Buzhi seated among them.
Overcome with joy, he could not help but dance. He then said to him: "This single scroll—"
Each word and every phrase exhaustively captures the subtleties of both the mundane and the supramundane; these are not merely the flowery rhetoric of the present age.

Yet, you do not know the point where one most urgently benefits others—do you understand this, my son? Yuan remained silent for a long time and said, "To cut directly to the root and set foot upon solid ground, nothing surpasses this.
As for withdrawing one's countenance into silent illumination, abiding in profound stillness without dependence, and probing the depths of the shallow and the deep—"
"Your lightness in coming and going is nothing more than a means of maintaining your person. I said, "Indeed.

However, during that time, while following the path of a worldly man, I saw a single branch or perhaps three or four blossoms of plum blooming by the side of a mountain stream in an ancient temple hidden within the wilderness.
I secretly marveled at this. What do you think of it? Yuan laughed and said, "I took you for a worldly man; now that I know it is so, you should treasure it all the more."

Inscription for a Painting of Herds of Cattle The rain has passed and the grass in the peach orchards is lush; To cease military expeditions and allow the herds to graze is most fitting. With heads held high and horns upon them, the herd rejoices together;
It is a joy to behold this era of great peace and tranquility.
Inscription on a Painting of Grass Insects:
Tall stalks and short stalks, the fragrant grasses are verdant; This one to the east, that one to the west, the autumn insects shiver in the cold.
A single expanse of the patriarch’s field, plain and white— Let not people of this age mistake it for a mere painting.
The First Seat, Master Lún, held the torch for the minor funeral rites at sixty-eight years of age.
To the north of the Northern Mountain and before the Southern Mountain, the wind was clear and the moon bright; from north to south, there was not even a hair’s breadth of difference.
No separation. With a single stroke of thunder, one’s entire life is lost, not a single star remains. The cliffs collapse and the rocks split;
the waters of Luojiang flow on, a continuous azure reaching the heavens. These are the final words of the Head Seat Moon-Rock (Yueyan).
I, this mountain monk, have followed them to break through [the barrier]. Does this accord with the truth? If it does not yet, I shall bind it again with verse, striking a circle with a torch.
Xiangyun said: "Do you see? When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and not even a hair-tip remains, the moon-disk remains solitary before the cliff.

When the monk Yue holds up a torch, once he sees the moon, he ceases to look at the finger; yet the moon still remains. Once he has returned home, he stops asking about the journey; yet the home still remains. Just so...
The birds cry out and the moon sets; when the house is broken and the people are gone, what then? The whole body is fire, the whole body is water;
amidst a mass of blazing flames, one beats up the raging waves.
Thus, the Venerable One holds aloft the torch (at the Lantern Festival).
Seeing that it is already established as existent is an old public case; one must grasp it to the death and examine it from every angle. With a "crack" it breaks, and with a "snap" it is severed.

The Lantern Festival is certainly on the fifteenth day of the first month. Walking along for no particular reason, one’s arm swings out and one mistakenly enters Chang’an. Lamps and fires burn through the void, snatching away the chill of night.
When the True Elder entered the stupa, his skin and flesh fell away until only the reality remained. Like a pearl or jade, it illuminated both heaven and earth;
the great earth could not conceal it, and impermanence could not swallow it. It fell into the hands of Xuefeng—tell me, how was this?
Distributing the portions: one part is offered to Śākyamuni Buddha; one part is offered to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha.
The Venerable Director of Affairs (Guǎng Weí-nà) holds a torch and, brandishing it in a circular motion, says: "Do you understand this? Its vastness matches heaven and earth; its radiance..."
Beyond sun and moon, the Buddha’s eye cannot pierce it; the Buddha’s hand cannot block it. With a single blow, it shatters into a hundred fragments.
Where can one seek its traces? Throwing down the torch, he said: "It is bright within the flash of a flint."
The Venerable Master held up a torch and, tracing a circle with it, asked, "Does anyone understand? This very moment is neither contemplating good nor contemplating evil;
it is one's original face before one’s parents were born. If you can grasp it in this way, then it is so.
Awakening from sleep, like a lotus blooming, like a sick person breaking into a sweat, like the dead returning to life—one attains it once and attains it forever, never again to regress.
Even so, if you hesitate or deliberate, the fiery serpent will burn your face.

The Venerable Jia took up the torch and cast off his official career, retiring to the forest. There he neither grasped at horizontal blades of grass nor held onto upright ones; coming and going were entirely at his own ease.
Wandering freely through birth and death, he rolls a brocade ball amidst a mass of blazing flames.
Abbot Guidu holds up a torch and says to me, "I am old and deaf;
I entrust you to serve as my arm and elbow. Together let us support this broken sand-pot and establish the school of Huangbo."
"This matter was not yet resolved when sudden destruction and change arrived. I was only then sighing over it as a single dream, yet you had already traveled a thousand li.
Though I pulled, I could not hold you back; though I called, you would not rise. Where have you gone? Raising a torch, he said:
So it is right here. [He draws a circle with his staff and asks: "Do you see? The nose straight, the eyes askance—vividly alive!
This is the white ox-cart of the High Vehicle, roaming freely before the gate of the burning house."
The poison of the "poisonous fruit" ignited by Xitang’s torch is no ordinary kind of venom; it is beyond comparison with the *liji* thorn and difficult even to liken to the *vajra*-circle.
When one smells it at the crown of the head, it severs the life-root of countless monks; when one gazes upon it with the eyes, it withers and suppresses them.
Furthermore, he saw skulls scattered across the ground; now they have all perished. Raising his torch, he said, "The kernel still remains.
Throwing it down, he said, "Cast it into the vast, crimson flames! Let its poisonous vapors fill the universe."
In self-praise:
My young disciple Huilin’s grandson, Faji, requests that I speak.

Though my teeth have fallen out and my head is grey, though my eyes are dim and my ears are deaf, I have not forgotten my favorite: the dried dung pellet. I cannot yet bear to lightly cast aside the chestnut.
The thorny burr: by means of this one sits amidst the forest thickets; by means of this one delivers the poor and destitute.
It is precisely because it is true and not empty that filial sons and compassionate grandsons have had its likeness written and its form painted.

Qiduguan invited Mushi to humble himself and guard his conduct with the compass. Amidst thunderclaps and gales, he remained as immovable as iron and stone; even if Mount Sumeru were to collapse, he would hold it up with a single hand.
Within the flash of lightning and the spark from flint, he drove the plow and seized the food; amidst the gentle breezes of spring, he shattered the withered and pulled down the decaying.
The wisdom of the mind that utterly transcends all things is known by few in the entire land. Those who do know it recognize the extraordinary nature of Mount Uṣṭra at the Zifu Prefecture.
My junior disciple Huizhang requested that I look upon him;
thus I wander through the world like a cloud in the sky, dwelling or departing as circumstances arise, without forming any thought of going or staying.
North and south, he follows his destination; east and west, he has no fixed direction. Having few skillful means as a person, he strikes one’s cheek with his palm at the slightest movement.
If that is how he goes about, how can the Master from beneath the mud and water be called Master Huankxi?
Xuefeng’s transformational spirit invited Lala Jujia:
carefree and detached, he was as warm as the springtime even during the harshest cold; in moments of extreme urgency, he was as expansive as the great ocean.
As soon as he opened his mouth, he would mock those who habitually speak empty words and resent those who slander Prajñā for no reason. At times...
He utters a single phrase of local dialect; even the Buddha cannot perceive its seams or cracks. From of old, Min and Shu have shared the same customs;
when they meet, there will naturally be those who understand them.

The Zen practitioner requests a praise for the red-earth painted winnowing basket: with a winter melon serving as the pestle-head, it pounds the iron caltrops to pieces and winnows out the long-grained rice.
There is no need for sifting, nor for cooking to satiety; throughout all generations, no one knows this.
Proofread by the Bhikṣu Puming, Abbot of Tiantong Jingde Chan Temple on Mount Taibai.
The Collected Records of Master Huankxi, Volume Lower (Concluded). Biographical Account.
The Master’s name was Weiyi; Huankxi was his self-appellation. He was the son of the Jia family of Mochi in Zizhou; his father was Chong and his mother Shi.
While she was pregnant, there were frequent auspicious omens. At his birth, he was calm and composed. When he was only ten years old, a great epidemic broke out in the village;
both the Master and his mother fell ill. As his mother’s illness reached its critical stage, she took the Master’s hand and said to his father, "Although my son is young, his natural disposition is—"

In all things, he never acted as a subordinate to others; one should observe him with care. Soon after, there was a monk named Juekai from Fanye Monastery in a nearby town who beheld the Master’s extraordinary features and requested that he become his novice. His father joyfully relinquished him to serve him.

At the age of twelve, while his father was on his way to the temple to offer incense at the shrine of Lord Zhang, he saw that the Master was exceptionally intelligent and quick-witted. It happened to be evening, and the Master had lit a lamp before the Buddha.
Xiangquan countered with the line: "Lighting a lamp, one recognizes this lamp. The Master immediately replied: "Pointing to the moon, one knows it is not the moon.
Xiangquan was greatly delighted and promised that on another day he would sell his monastic certificate to make him his disciple and grant him the tonsure.

Subsequently, when he followed his paternal uncle Ju Yuanheng to study and associated with the local scholar Zheng Dehou, he already displayed a towering presence and the marks of a great talent. Thus...

He practiced the examination curriculum and accompanied his father’s officials on the annual tribute mission. In his early twenties, while receiving the *quan* (liquor) and fruit from Shi Xiangquan as per imperial decree, he abandoned his studies and shaved his head.
He received full ordination at Gānlù Monastery in Chengdu. Subsequently, he went to Língyún to thank Xiangquan;
Xiangquan urged him to travel abroad for study. At twenty-two, he visited the lecture hall of Dàcí Monastery, where he realized that his current understanding was not yet exhaustive.
Having finished [his studies], he then departed to visit Master Huì'ān Guāng at Zhèngfǎ, Master Nùtáng Biàn at Liùzǔ, and Master Tǔ'ān Guī at Dōnglín;
he went to all of them to seek instruction and resolution. Day and night, he applied himself with tireless diligence to investigate and clarify his own fundamental matter.
One day, while the venerable Shānjiāng Huì visited him, the Master asked: "The nature of wind is eternally abiding; it is nowhere not pervasive."
"What was the meaning of the ancients' fanning? Huì said, "I have told you all at once. The Master remained silent for a long time.
He escorted Huì back as far as Dà'ān Gate, then turned back at Dàfú Street. As he walked, the Master said to himself, "What was the meaning of the ancients' fanning?
Suddenly, he attained realization and said, "Picking up gold on the main street; the four neighbors..."

How could he have known? Overjoyed beyond measure, he returned home and told Tu’an. Tu’an said, “This is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the clarification of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Body and mind are light and at ease; though lacking wisdom, one restrains oneself naturally. If you awaken to this, there will be no fault.”

"This does not constitute the realization of a sage. At this, the Master’s joyful expression suddenly vanished. The following day, in the earthen hut, the Hermit asked the Master, "What is the Buddha?
The Master lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Hermit said, "As long as you have a sitting cloth, I will follow you;

but when you have no sitting cloth, what then? The Master gave him a fist-blow straight to the chest. The Hermit pushed him away and said, "Come back here and pull the tiger's whiskers! The Master... [proceeded].
[The Master] said, "This is not beyond my capacity. Subsequently, he followed Netang at the Sixth Patriarch’s [monastery] and Tusan at Zhengfa.
From then on, their words were in harmony and their spiritual affinities were perfectly matched; both elders clapped their hands in approval and praised him.
Since the study of Direct Pointing was flourishing in the south, the Master took passage by boat eastward to exit the Gorges, arriving first at Eiseng (Two Saints) in Gong’an.
Not long after, he departed to travel to Mount Nanyue. There he encountered Master Wuer, who was just entering the Fuyan Hall.
Inside the room, Wuer asked the Master, "What thing comes like this? The Master said, "I do not know. Wuer said, "Dharma has arrived. The Master then said, "Take care."

Wu’er said, “It is so; it is indeed so. The Master said, “Do not conceal your brilliance. Wu’er merely smiled. Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Lu and entered Zhejiang, passing through Suzhou and Huzhou until he reached Hangzhou.
There he heard that Chan Master Fojian was residing at Yuyang Monastery, and that his reputation for the Way had spread far and wide.
He then crossed the river to visit Yujia (Jueji). At that time, students from the four quarters came to study, rushing like clouds and flowing like water;

those who sought to enter the hall often waited for months or even ten days without success. Those who did gain entry were as rare as one ascending the Dragon Gate. The Master went directly to the abbot’s quarters with incense in hand to have an audience.
Fojian observed the Master’s dignified and robust bearing and recognized him as a vessel of the Dharma. That very day, he was admitted to the hall, to the great astonishment of the assembly.
[The Master] was surprised. Later, when [the Master] entered the room, Fojian asked him, "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi?
The Master replied, "When the dragon roars, the mist rises. Fojian said, "I ask you this: why was the Bodhisattva Wuming of the lower realm able to emerge from the woman’s samādhi?
[The Master] replied, "When the tiger roars, the wind arises. Fojian said, "You certainly say so. The Master said: [He agreed].
"I do not act in such a manner," [the Master] said. Fojian asked, "And how would you act? The Master replied, "When the tiger roars, the wind arises.
Fojian said, "How could a shrimp ever leap out of its basket? The Master responded again, "How can even the Master himself avoid being caught in doubt?
Fojian then struck him. Several months later, he had the Master attend to the incense. When Fojian moved to Mount Jing, he further appointed the Master as the Librarian (Zhizang).
He traveled to Jinling, where he stayed with Master Chijue Chong at Zhongfu for two years. Upon returning to Jingshan, he was subsequently appointed to lead the assembly.
In the year of Bingwu during the Chunyou era, the seat of Ruiyan in Jianning was vacant;

the Prefectural Governor, Imperial Academician Yang Gonghui, commissioned the Elder Yi of Qingxi at Kaiyuan Temple to recommend a man of realized virtue to preside over it. Yi recommended the Master, who was selected from among the candidates.

Lord Yang earnestly invited him to open the hall for formal teachings, where he offered incense before the Buddha Juejian. Shortly thereafter, Governor Song Zhi invited the Master to reside at Lianfeng Hermitage.
Before long, he moved to Huili Temple in Linjiang, and subsequently to Baofeng Temple in Hongzhou.
When Lord Weng Fu, the Commissioner of Jiangxi, promoted him, the Master took up residence at Huanglong. After five years, he retired to Shushan in Linchuan.
Huang Gong (Ke), the Right Minister of the Guard, invited the Master to reside at Beichan in the prefecture, but he did not accept.

Subsequently, Qian Gong (Yingsun), the Prefectural Governor of Jianchang, invited the Master to reside at Zisheng. Hong Gong (Shou), the Commissioner of the Transport Office, then transferred the Master to Huangbo in Junzhou.
He stayed at each for one year before retiring back to Ganshan. Cao Gong (Xiaqing), the Commissioner of the Fiscal Office, again [invited him] with the same [offer].
At Shanglan, he invited Master Yan, who declined and would not accept the summons. At that time, the seat at Mount Yangshan in Yuan was vacant; the Zhizhi Hall raised the Master to fill the position.
Once the imperial decree had been issued, the Master could not decline it. He remained there for five years before being transferred to Xuefeng in Fuzhou.
Another five years passed until he received an edict to move to Tiantong in Mingzhou. Originally, Tiantong had been expanded from Shifan.
When the Duke passed away, the Grand Tutor and Chancellor, Lord Jia of Wei State, entered Yanfu Monastery to provide a vegetarian feast for the monks.

Among the assembly of Chan practitioners from the mountains and rivers selected by Master Jiao Zhushan, all set their hearts upon this master. When the lot was drawn, the sound of joyous acclaim was like rolling thunder.
Monks from both the Northern and Southern mountains packed their bags and traveled to the eastern region, waiting for his arrival; they numbered no fewer than a hundred. The monastic community—
Such prosperity had never been seen before. Not long after, the temple was suddenly struck by fire.
The Master personally braved the wind and rain, wandering for alms through the western districts and obtaining tens of millions in gold coins. He then planned to restore the temple;

yet even amidst these calamities, he remained diligent and untiring in maintaining the community and practicing the Way. All that pertains to the duties of a *jūji* (abbot), which ought to be performed, he carried out.

It was not because his illness was grave that he ever ceased [his practice] for even a moment. When the Yuan dynasty underwent its transformation [the establishment of the new reign], everyone everywhere bowed their heads like grass before the wind, prostrating themselves at the gates of power.

The Master alone maintained his integrity and did not yield. Consequently, eminent officials and great ministers of the time, such as Imperial Commissioner Yu Huang Gong (Zhen) and the former Magistrate of Yongjia County Chen Gong (Meng), both sent letters to recommend and praise him. In his old age and illness, he declined his official duties and retired to the Eastern Hall. Previously, in the autumn of the Bingzi year, the Master had fallen ill;
he then instructed his disciples to find a plot of ground on the western side of the temple and build a small cottage of several rafters as a place for his final repose.

The hills and ridges faced it, standing out beautifully and worth beholding. Consequently, he took the name "White Lotus Peak" from a local landmark to name the hermitage, thereby demonstrating [his intent].

In accordance with the intention of returning to one’s ancestral grave, on the first day of the ninth month of the autumn in the year of Xinsi, he suddenly instructed his disciples to prepare for his final departure.
Four days later, he requested a bath, changed his robes, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. On that day, there was a great wind and rain, and the clouds were dark and gloomy.
The following day, the sky cleared and brightened. Those arriving from all quarters to attend the funeral followed one after another in continuous succession;

the onlookers were like a wall of people. The grandeur of the funeral rites was unprecedented. The remains were kept in the shrine for seven days, after which his disciples escorted the whole body to be interred on the mountain behind the monastery, in accordance with the Master’s own wishes.
His secular age was eighty, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*) was sixty. He ordained several disciples.
The number of his dharma heirs was several; Nanhua Ketang Wuyue was the foremost among them, yet those who came to him have not ceased to this day.
As for the Master’s character: his physical build was imposing and robust, his voice resonant and clear, and his countenance grave and stern.
He did not speak frivolously. In his leisure time at home, he sat upright and in silence, gazing with the intense stare of a tiger; people looked upon him with awe. Whenever he ascended [the hall]...
Seated upon the lion throne, he held the fly-whisk while instructing his disciples; like water pouring from a vessel or clouds rising in the sky, his teaching flowed without obstruction.

His style was a refined blend of literary elegance and plain substance, such that those who listened forgot their weariness. Within the hall, he was particularly unyielding, never granting permission lightly.

When students presented their understanding through verses or hymns, they invariably met with his rebukes and scoldings. He showed no favoritism or partiality, remaining impartial toward all throughout his tenure as abbot.
Whatever offerings and benefits he received, he gave them away as soon as they were obtained. During his time in the Eastern Hall, he again exhausted all that he possessed to distribute as gifts;
he even donated his own robes to assist in the construction project. He took nothing more than what was necessary for his basic needs thereafter. Master Jue once remarked:

The Way of Fojian was like a great dragon pouring forth rain everywhere; moistened by this single rain, there was no discrimination whatsoever, yet the grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, and shrubs each received benefits according to their own capacities and natures.

Now, those who are successors of Fojian and have been commissioned by imperial decree to oversee the Great Temple (Dazhaoti) stand one after another, facing each other back-to-back, towering and prominent before the eyes and ears of the people. As for the clarity of cause and effect, it is self-evident.
His practice and understanding were in accord, and he was proficient in both the essential tenets and their exposition; the Master may truly be said to have possessed both.

As for his preaching in accordance with the capacities of others and his proclamation of the fundamental vehicle (zongcheng), these are fully recorded in the *Jiuhui Lu*. Having been by the Master’s side in the past, I am well-acquainted with his life and conduct.
Now, having been humbly entrusted with this account of his deeds, I shall not neglect this humble task but shall respectfully compose these lines. *Feijing Ba* (Humble Respectful One Hundred).
With prostrations and bowed heads, I have recorded these events exactly as they occurred.
I relate them without composing anything new, seeking that those who are the great calligraphers of this age might engrave them upon metal and stone to manifest them for eternity.

Now, observing Master Huánxī’s *Jiùhuì Lù* (Record of the Nine Assemblies), it may truly be said that his preaching responded to capacities like thunder and lightning, and responded to the occasion like clouds and rain.

From the beginning of the first fascicle to the end of the last, if one carefully examines and collates it, is it not the case that his preaching was like thunder and lightning, and like clouds and rain?
Indeed. Therefore, when I was serving my late master at that time, I witnessed this auspicious sign in the world.
The Master then struck the drum to assemble the assembly and, with both hands, entrusted me with the three-pound heavy-bottomed staff transmitted by his predecessors.

From then on, I held it up alone and wielded it exclusively, displaying its full range of expressive gestures; only then did its true nature become manifest. Thus, the one who bestowed it did not bestow it in vain, and I received it accordingly.

Those who do so likewise shall not receive [the teaching] in vain. Those who peruse this record should cast their eyes beyond the words; then they will truly know that the Way does not reside merely in these texts.
